In this unit 'The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)'
LEARNING INTENTIONS

You will listen: to a dialogue, to ask and respond to questions of personal interest • You will speak: a dialogue • You will read: 'Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)' • You will learn: silent letters, syllables, long and short vowel sounds • You will write: summary through given mind map
Listening & Speaking
Ask and respond to questions of personal interest. Work in pairs and practice the dialogue below to ask and respond to questions of personal interest.
Listening & Speaking
Nida: Asalam-o-Aliakum Sara! Are you interested in reading Islamic History?
Listening & Speaking
Sara: Walaik-um-Asalam Nida! Yes, I have a passion for reading Islamic History.
Listening & Speaking
Nida: Ok good, do you read it now-a-days?
Listening & Speaking
Sara: Yeah, I have got a book from my uncle?
Listening & Speaking
Nida: Great! Do you want to visit the library for getting some books?
Listening & Speaking
Sara: Of course, why not. We'll find a lot of our interest there.
Listening & Speaking
Nida: Really! I think we should then go tomorrow.
Reading
In pairs, discuss the following:
Reading

Why did non-Muslims trust Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ)? • How did Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) set high and noble ideals for all mankind? • How can people achieve perfection in the moral, spiritual and social areas of life?
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)
In the Qur'an, Allah (SWT) commands believers:
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

"O believers! Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives. Be they rich or poor, Allah is best to ensure their interests. So do not let your desires cause you to deviate from justice. If you distort the testimony or refuse to give it, then know that Allah is certainly All-Aware of what you do." (Surat an-Nisa, 4:135)
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)
Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) abided by Allah's (SWT) commands, even before he (ﷺ) was entrusted with the duty of nabuwwat, justice was instilled in him as a result of divine training.
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

From the time of his childhood, Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) remained outside the moral degeneration of the societies in the 'Age of Ignorance.' He (ﷺ) opposed oppression and injustice in his youth, and he (ﷺ) joined the pact of social justice, 'Hilful-Fudul' an association, formed for fair commercial dealing in pre-Islamic Makkah. 'Hulf' means oath whereas 'Fudul' means people with virtue.
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

Before Islam, justice system was not based on a sound foundation among the Arabs. There was no written law to be taken as a basis for implementation, therefore, resolving conflicts was left to the discretion of judges. However, the decision was not absolute, because the powerful might not conform to judgments against them. For this reason, the weak were usually found guilty.
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) based the Justice system on the principle of giving a person his / her due; no matter whatever his / her stature may be; dominant or oppressed. During Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) time, a cottage was built on a piece of land belonging to two brothers. The heirs disputed the ownership of the cottage. They went to the Rasool (ﷺ) to resolve the issue.
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

The beloved Rasool (ﷺ) assigned Hazrat Huzaifa Bin Yaman (RA) to handle the case. Hazrat Huzaifa (RA) went to the site of the cottage for investigation. He (RA) recorded statements of various people, took evidences from witnesses and presented his decision to Hazrat Muhammad
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)
...Rasoolullah (ﷺ) for his approval. He (ﷺ) considered the decision and approved it.
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

In the institution of justice established by Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ), the judge makes decision according to evidence; thus, a wrong cannot be made right with his decision. For this reason false witnessing and presenting unfounded evidence are strongly forbidden. Deceiving a judge to get a decision in one's favour is referred to as "A piece of fire" by the beloved Rasool (ﷺ).
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)
The Holy Quran instructs the Muslims to maintain justice even when dealing with their enemies:
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

"O you who believe, be maintainers of justice (and bearer of witness for (the sake of) God. Let not hatred of a people incite you to act unjustly; be just this is nearer to righteousness. And fear God surely God is aware of what you do." (Surah al-Maida, 5:8)
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

As head of the state of Madinah, Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) would decide all cases on merit with justice and fairness. Once a Quraish woman was found guilty of stealing; some people wanted to save her from punishment in order to protect the honor of the family of Quraish. They wanted to hush up the whole affair.
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

They asked Hazrat Osama bin Zaid (RA), who was very dear to the Rasool (ﷺ), to intercede on her behalf. Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) became very angry and said, "Bani Israel was ruined because of this. They applied law to the poor and forgave the rich". During a Sermon, an Ansari, seeing some men from the tribe Banu Tha'lba stood up and pointed towards them and said, "Oh Rasoolullah (ﷺ)!
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

Their ancestor killed a member of our family. We appeal to you to get one of them hanged in exchange of that. Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) replied, "The revenge of the father cannot be taken on his son."
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

Hazrat Muhammad Rasoolullah (ﷺ) proved by his own example that no one could be more firm for justice than him, even if it was against his own interest or the interest of those who were near and dear to him. He (ﷺ) decided every case brought to him, by friend or foe, with justice, without fear or favour. A person of such magnitude transcends the barriers of time and space.
The Justice of Rasoolullah (ﷺ)

People of all ages can find something in his life to provide them with guidance in various fields. The Holy Quran clearly mentions this aspect of his life, in these words: "There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often." (Quran 33:21)

amination of the facts about a situation, crime etc.; ignorance | a lack of knowledge or information about something; fairness | the quality of treating people equally or in a way that is reasonable; barrier | an object like a fence that prevents people from moving forward from one place to another

Use of Language: Long and short vowel sounds

When a vowel sounds like its name, this is called a long sound. A vowel letter can also have short sounds. Whether a vowel has a long sound, a short sound, or remains silent, depends on its position in a word and the letters around it.
Short Vowels
The most common sound for each vowel is its "short" sound:
Short Vowels

ă, pronounced /æ/ as in apple, pan, or mat • ĕ, pronounced /ɛ/ as in elephant, pen, or met • ĭ, pronounced /ɪ/ as in insect, pin, or mitt • ŏ, pronounced /ɒ/ as in octopus, ostrich, upon, or motto • ŭ, pronounced /ʌ/ as in umbrella, pun, or mutt

Unit 2: Living Together
In pairs, discuss what each of the following pictures signifies, communicates or represents.
Side note

The world is facing issues like never before. War stricken countries; hunger and global warming to name a few. Peaceful co-existence has become difficult to achieve. Young minds must learn to live and let others live, tolerate differences and celebrate equality to overcome this issue.
FRIENDS
Listening: Take turns and read this text aloud. Be sensitive to other speakers. Do not speak when someone else is speaking. Listen carefully when someone is speaking aloud.
FRIENDS

"A Time to Talk" (By: Robert Frost): WHEN a friend calls to me from the road / And slows his horse to a meaning walk, / I don't stand still and look around / On all the hills I haven't hoed, / And shout from where I am, What is it? / No, not as there is a time to talk. / I thrust my hoe in the mellow ground, / Blade-end up and five feet tall, / And plod: I go up to the stone wall / For a friendly visit.
Can you do it?

Use the word, 'FRIENDS' and come up with an acrostic poem. Remember an acrostic poem is a set of letters (as the first letter of the lines) taken in order from a word or phrase. Generally, the letters of the words are written vertically.
Can you do it?
F · R · I · E · N · D · S
Vocabulary
Use contextual clues to figure out the meanings. Remember that it is not necessary to know the definitions of all the words in the poem to understand the poem's meaning.
Tips for Teachers

Ask students to read the poem aloud in groups. Talk with your group about the imagery, or what you see in this poem, as you answer the given questions. Each group member should read the poem aloud at least once.
Speaking

In pairs, discuss the following questions with your partner and present your findings in the form of a presentation to the class. The presentation can be on a chart paper or powerpoint etc. A presentation can be different based on your audience. You need to present precise information that your audience can understand and enjoy. To do this, you need to plan it carefully.
Speaking

Present continuous

There are various ways you can in which you can express events occurring in the future including the present continuous, 'be going to', 'will' and 'shall'. Use of 'going to' and 'will / shall'

Text 2-A: Deforestation

Deforestation is the destruction of native forests and woods on a long-term basis. It is a very severe problem with several consequences for the ecosystem. It happens when humans cut trees for their own needs. Even if it is to meet human requirements, it cannot be justified because it poses a significant threat to the environment's biodiversity. Biodiversity is critical to the ecosystem's overall health.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Forests are necessary for maintaining and sustaining global ecosystems, so we must safeguard them. Many living species rely on forests for their survival. They provide humans with a wide range of gifts that improve our quality of life. They take CO₂ from the atmosphere and generate oxygen, which is required by living creatures.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Natural phenomena also account for deforestation. Volcanic eruptions, for example, can burn away the wood lands surrounding the volcano. Some other natural phenomena of deforestation are storms, floods, attack of parasites on plants, and lightening etc.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Agriculture and cattle grazing are two of the primary causes of deforestation. To meet the ever increasing demand for food, forest area is regularly destroyed and converted to agricultural land (which can, in turn, be linked to overpopulation). Palm oil, lumber, soy, and cattle are the four key commodities responsible for tropical deforestation.
Text 2-A: Deforestation
Another major driver of deforestation is the creation of grazing land for livestock.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Forests act as carbon sinks by absorbing atmospheric CO₂ during photosynthesis. Because carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, deforestation contributes directly to the greenhouse effect and (as a result) global warming. Tree roots tend to attach to the soil bedrock, strengthening the soil. Additionally, the plant litter produced by trees protects the soil's surface.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

When trees are removed (due to deforestation), the soil becomes prone to erosion. Landslides are frequently associated with sloped terrain deforestation, which can be explained by the loss of soil adhesion caused by the absence of trees. Natural disasters, such as floods, amplify the extent of erosion (note that the plant litter found on forest surfaces helps reduce the amount of soil washed away).
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Forests are home to a diverse range of species. Tropical rainforests are thought to have the most diverse ecosystems in the world. Deforestation is a significant danger to this biodiversity. Locally, forest area removal might lead to a reduction in the number of certain species. However, on a global basis, deforestation can lead to the extinction of some desirable species.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Every year, around 50,000 species (including plants, animals, and insects) are lost due to deforestation. According to studies, approximately 40% of all plant and animal species in Southeast Asia will become extinct throughout the twenty-first century. The consequences of large scale biodiversity loss are difficult to foresee, but they are quite likely.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Forests cover 31 percent of the earth's surface or around 4.06 billion hectares. Only 18% of the world's forests are protected against destruction. Since 1990, around 420 million hectares of forest have gone. Every year between 1990 and 2010, an average of 15.5 million hectares of forest were lost.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

Between 2010 and 2015, 12 million hectares of forest were lost each year, representing a 22.58 percent decrease from 1990 to 2010. Between 2015 and 2020, 10 million hectares of forest were burned each year, representing a 35.48 percent decline from 1990 to 2010 and a 16.67 percent decline from 2010 to 2015. Every minute, 2,400 trees are felled.
Text 2-A: Deforestation
Another three hectares of forest will have been cleared by the time you finish reading this phrase.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

After Pakistan attained independence in the late 1940s, woods covered 33 percent of the country. However, according to Ministry of Climate Change data from 2015, barely 5% of the country now has tree cover. According to some non-governmental assessments, present forest cover is actually lower at 3%.
Text 2-A: Deforestation

After years of deforestation, Pakistan's government is focusing on large scale 'afforestation.' Since June 2015, the "Billion Tree Tsunami" project has been striving to save Pakistan's forests in two ways: to prevent future deforestation and to repair past harm by planting saplings. 250 million saplings have been planted in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in the last year, greatly exceeding the average annual count of 20 million.

Use of Language: What is a Phrasal Verb?

A phrasal verb is usually two or three words. The first word is a verb, and the other word or words are prepositions. When you use the words together, the phrase has a specific meaning. Often, the meaning is related to the meaning of the verb, but not always. For example, 'blow up' can mean "to put air into something" like a balloon or a tire. Use of Language: Complex and Compound Sentences
A clause is a group of words and sentences are made up of clauses. A simple sentence has just one clause. It expresses one thought. Example: The tunnel sits 190 m below sea level.
Points to know

A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and one or more dependent clauses connected to it. A dependent clause is a clause that does not express a complete thought. Examples of dependent clauses: a) while he waited for the drink b) although they share some similar properties c) whenever he talks about that experience
Use of Language: Complex and Compound Sentences
A compound sentence joins simple sentences together, using words like and, or, but, so, yet, nor, for. Example: The tunnel sits 190 m below the sea level, and connects two continents.
Complex Sentences

In complex sentences, the clauses are connected by subordinating conjunctions. Some common subordinating conjunctions include when, until, because, while, if, although, after, as, before, whenever, since, and whereas. An independent clause is joined with one or more dependent clause by a subordinating conjunction to form a complex sentence.
Complex Sentences

Independent clause: He realised that the bus was late. Dependent Clause: While he was waiting at the bus station. Complex sentence: He realised that the bus was late while he was waiting at the bus station.
Complex Sentences

You can construct a complex sentence by including the dependent clause first, followed by the independent clause. Example: When I told him that I was resigning from the job, he was shocked. You can also write the independent clause first, followed by the dependent clause, as given below.
Points to know: Remember!

A simple sentence has one subject and one predicate. A compound sentence is made up of two or more independent clauses. It contains two or more simple sentences joined by a comma 'and', 'but', 'or'. They can also be joined by a semicolon (;).
Points to know: Remember!

Commas are needed within sentences to separate the items in a list or different grammatical parts for example, they are extensively used in complex sentences. Comma can be put before a clause beginning with 'and', 'but', 'so', and 'or'.

Use of Language: Active voice and Passive voice

Voice refers to the form of a verb that indicates when a grammatical subject performs the action or is the receiver of the action. When a sentence is written in the active voice, the subject performs the action. When the sentence is written in the passive voice, the subject receives the action.

Use of Language: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives

Certain adjectives compare two or more nouns or pronouns. The comparative form of an adjective compares two things or people. It is usually formed by adding -er to an adjective that has only one syllable. If an adjective has more than one syllable, the comparative is usually formed by adding the word more before the adjective.
Use of Language: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives
Example: Ali is older than his brother, Fahad. The long coat is more expensive than the short one.
Use of Language: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives

The superlative form of an adjective compares more than two people or things. It is usually formed by adding -est to an adjective that has only one syllable. If the adjective has more than one syllable, the superlative is usually formed by adding 'most' before the adjective.
Use of Language: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives
Example: Peter is the oldest of the three Mayor's children. The long coat is the most expensive of all the coats. Example: ugly, uglier, ugliest; polite, politer, politest.
Use of Language: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives

For adjectives that end in 'y', change y to i before adding the suffixes ier and iest. Example: healthy, healthier, healthiest; windy, windier, windiest. Comparative and superlative adjectives can also be formed by adding the words 'more' (comparative) and 'most' (superlative) before the adjective.
Use of Language: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives
For example, Egypt is more famous than Greece. The statue of the Happy Prince was the most beautiful one in the city.

Punctuating statements and questions in direct speech: If a person has made a statement, then a coma comes before the speech marks in direct speech. "Dear swallow," called the Happy Prince sadly. If a person asks a question, the question mark comes before the speech marks. "Why are you weeping then?" asked the swallow.

You can also write the speech at the end of a sentence, using a comma before the speech marks begin. The children's faces grew rosier, "We have bread now!" they cried.

Text 1: We Are All One

In return, if you ever need our help, all you need do is call for us, and we will hear you and come to your aid." As the dream ended and the woman began to wake, she heard the queen ant's voice calling after her, distinctly saying, "We are all one."
Text 1: We Are All One

All through that day, the woman searched for the herb. She wondered if she were already too late - and if everyone in her village was already blind. She was startled from her thoughts by the sound of a bird, intent upon catching a small centipede. The centipede was scurrying across the ground as quickly as his multi legs would carry him.
Text 1: We Are All One

Taking pity upon the defenseless centipede, she quickly scooped him up and frightened the bird from her prey. Saying, "We are all one," she carried the centipede to some leaves and placed it gently in their cover.
Text 1: We Are All One

That night she again had strange dreams. This time she was visited by the centipede. "Thank you for saving my life," the tiny voice proclaimed. "And now I will help you as you helped me. The herb you seek can be found by an ancient oak tree, in the very center of the forest." An image of a gnarled and twisting trunk came to her mind as she heard the centipede state, "We are all one." Then she awoke.
Text 1: We Are All One

The woman spent the next morning making her way into the heart of the woods, searching for the oak tree. As the day progressed, she noticed that the trees around her were getting blurry. Gazing towards the sky, she saw that the sun was still high in the sky. With a dawning horror she realized that she, too, must have contracted the strange illness.
Text 1: We Are All One
Quickening her pace she continued toward the center of the forest, but with every step her eyesight worsened.
Text 1: We Are All One

Just as she was giving way to despair, she found the ancient oak tree! Even though she could barely see, she could tell it looked just like the one she had seen in her dream. Stumbling and out of breath, she began to search for the herb frantically. It was no use - her eyes could no longer tell one plant from another.
Text 1: We Are All One
Crying with frustration she wept for her husband, her children, herself, and the people of her village.
Text 1: We Are All One

She turned to try to retrace her steps to her home and then she remembered. The ants! Perhaps they could help her now. She called to them and soon enough small voices responded. "Bend down," the queen ant's voice called. "The herb you seek is right here. I am standing on it." Gently the woman knelt and reached towards the sound.
Text 1: We Are All One

With cautious movements so as not to harm the queen ant, she found the herb and plucked it. Slowly and carefully she tore a small piece of the leaf and chewed it. Almost instantaneously, her sight was restored. Joyfully she harvested the herbs and prepared to return to her village. Before she left, however, she thanked the ants and proclaimed one last time, "We are all one."
Text 1: We Are All One

The woman walked as swiftly as she could - all day and then all night, by the light of the moon. She hoped, oh, how she hoped, that she would return on time to save her village from blindness. Finally she reached her home. As she called to her children they followed her voice, for by now they were all completely blind. Anxiously she gave them bits of the herb and then she waited to see what would happen.
Text 1: We Are All One

One minute passed - and then another - and then her eldest son laughed with joy. "I see you!" he shouted, "I truly see you!" Soon everyone in the village had been cured of the strange illness and the woman who had saved them all returned to her simple but happy life with her husband and their three children. And she never forgot that "We are all one."

When we ask "Where might we find extraterrestrial life," the first place many scientists turn to, because of its similarity to the Earth, is Mars. Mars may have been like the Earth in its past. Although no signs of life on Mars have been found, scientists continue to search because they are aware of the potential for life in extreme environments.
Life on Mars?
A Martian meteorite fueled speculation and debate in 1996 when scientists reported that it held signs of past life. The search now moves to Mars itself.
Life on Mars?

In July, 1996, it was announced that Dr. David McKay, along with a team of scientists at Johnson Space Center (a division of NASA), had discovered possible fossils of bacteria in a meteorite named ALH84001 that came from Mars. It was found in the Allen Hills in Antarctica in 1984 after having landed there 12,000 years ago.
Life on Mars?

Scientists found that the rock, called ALH84001, had a peculiar chemical makeup. It contained a combination of minerals and carbon compounds that on Earth are created by microbes. It also had crystals of magnetic iron oxide, called magnetite, which some bacteria produce. Moreover, McKay presented to the crowd an electron microscope view of the rock showing chains of globules that bore a striking resemblance to chains
Life on Mars?

...that some bacteria form on Earth. "We believe that these are indeed microfossils from Mars," McKay said, adding that the evidence wasn't "absolute proof" of past Martian life but rather "pointers in that direction."
Life on Mars?

Several different chemicals and molecular structures were exciting because they looked similar to byproducts of life on Earth. However, these chemicals and structures can also be created without life. Some are even present in deep space on comets, and scientists do not think that they came from Martian life anymore.
Life on Mars?

NASA researchers are taking lessons from the debate about life on Earth to Mars. If all goes as planned, a new generation of rovers will arrive on Mars within the next decade. These missions will incorporate cutting-edge biotechnology designed to detect individual molecules made by Martian organisms, either living or long dead.
Life on Mars?

For life to exist on Mars, there must be liquid water. There is plenty of water on Mars, but most of it is frozen in the polar ice caps and buried underground. Despite the chilly temperatures, there could be liquid water underneath the surface ice in some places, since salt lowers the freezing point of water. Satellite data suggest there is a permanent lake, 20 kilometers across, hidden beneath the south pole.
Life on Mars?

The search for life on Mars has become more urgent, thanks in part to probes by the two rovers now roaming Mars' surface and another, spaceship that is orbiting the planet. In recent months, they've made a series of astonishing discoveries that, once again, tempt scientists to believe that Mars harbors life—or did so in the past.
Life on Mars?

At a February conference in the Netherlands, an audience of Mars experts was surveyed about Martian life. Some 75 percent of the scientists said they thought life once existed there, and of them, 25 percent think that Mars harbors life today.
Use of Language: Conjunctions

A conjunction is a word used to connect words, phrases and clauses. There are seven main conjunctions in the English language, which you can remember using the acronym FANBOYS: for, and, nor, neither, but, or, yet, and so.
Use of Language: Conjunctions

Coordinating conjunctions join words, phrases and independent clauses. Examples include: and, but, for, nor, or, so and yet. • Correlative conjunctions join words and phrases that have fairly equivalent weight in a sentence. They appear in pairs, such as either/or, neither/nor, and not only/but also.
Use of Language: Conjunctions

• Subordinating conjunctions join independent clauses to dependent clauses and indicate which is the main clause and which is subordinate clause. Examples: after, although, as, because, before, if, once, since, than, that, though, till, until, when, where, whether, while and yet.
Use of Language: Conjunctions
The main clause may be first in the sentence or second. The subordinate clause follows the subordinate conjunction so the main clause is emphasized.

Will robots ever replace humans?

Robot technology was an invention the aim of which, was to assist the human beings. Will robots ever replace humans?

Will robots ever replace humans?

Robotic Ambassador: Sophia - the most recognizable face of humanoids, was developed by Hong Kong-based Hanson Robotics. Taught by humans, Sophia can move, talk, show some emotions, draw, and sing. First activated on February 14, 2016, this humanoid robot continues her role as a robotic ambassador, helping to advance research into robotics and human-robot interactions.
Will robots ever replace humans?

Robotic Avatar: Initially introduced by Toyota in 2017, the T-HR3 is a humanoid robot that mimics the movements of its human operator—like a real world avatar. These humanoids will ideally be able to perform surgeries while their operators—human doctors—control them from another part of the world.
Will robots ever replace humans?
These humanoids will also allow caregivers to do their work remotely, and for those in need of assistance to live a more independent life.
Will robots ever replace humans?
Delivery robots: In January 2020, it was announced that Ford became the first customer to incorporate Agility Robotics' humanoid robot, called Digit, into a factory setting.
Will robots ever replace humans?

This headless humanoid has nimble limbs which can pick up and stack boxes weighing up to 40 pounds, and sensors that allow it to navigate various obstacles such as stairs and varying terrains. Will robots ever replace humans?
Ford envisions that Digit will be able to ride in a driverless car and deliver packages to customers, automating the entire delivery process.
Will robots ever replace humans?

PARO: The Therapeutic Robot: It is a well-known fact that pets and cute animals help to ease stress; to divert attention from pain and to reduce the feeling of loneliness. Will robots ever replace humans?

It allows the documented benefits of animal therapy to be administered to patients in environments such as hospitals and extended care facilities where live animals present treatment or logistical difficulties.
Will robots ever replace humans?

PARO has been found to reduce patient stress and their caregivers; stimulates interaction between patients and caregivers; has been shown to have a psychological effect on patients, improving their relaxation and motivation; improves the socializiation of patients with each other and with caregivers; and considered as the World's Most Therapeutic Robot certified by Guinness World Records.

Use of Language: Independent & Dependent Clauses

An independent clause is a group of words with a subject and a predicate that expresses a complete thought and can stand by itself as a sentence. Example (independent clause): Iceland is the 'healthiest country in the world' because they have higher life-expectancy.
Use of Language: Independent & Dependent Clauses

A dependent clause cannot stand alone. It depends upon the independent clause of the sentence to complete its meaning. Dependent clauses start with words like who, which, that, because, when, if, until, before and after. Example (dependent clause): It improves the function of blood vessels and increases blood flow, which can help protect us against a heart attack and other cardiovascular problems.

A Healthy Living for Everyone

Many of the serious health concerns in today's world can be linked to poor diet. People who regularly consume food high in sodium, sugar, and saturated fat not only increase their chances of obesity, but also increase their risk of developing heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, and several types of cancer.
A Healthy Living for Everyone
Although some people who regularly consume unhealthy foods do so knowingly, there is also a significant portion of the population that remains undereducated about proper nutrition.
A Healthy Living for Everyone

The department of Agriculture in USA has prepared a food guide to help people learn about which types of food are the healthiest to eat. The food guide describes six basic food groups: meat (beef, fish, chicken, etc.), dairy (milk, yogurt, cheese, etc.), grains (bread, cereal, rice, etc.), fruit, and vegetables. The last group is fats, oil, and sweets.
A Healthy Living for Everyone

It also suggests how much of each food group is healthy to eat daily. Doctors believe that fruit and vegetables can actually prevent many different diseases. On the other hand, animal fat can cause diseases.
A Healthy Living for Everyone

People who eat a lot of meat and only a small amount of grains, fruit, and vegetables have a high rate of cancer and heart disease. In Japan, in contrast, people eat large amounts of grains and very little meat. The Japanese also have a very low rate of cancer and heart disease. In fact, the Japanese live longer than almost anyone else in the world.

Exercise is just as important for children and the elderly as it is for adults. Vigorous physical activity aids in children's overall development so they reach optimal size and functional capacities in adulthood. Exercise benefits for the elderly include increased strength, flexibility, and mobility. These benefits in turn help with balance and can minimise the risk of falls and the injuries resulting from them.
A Healthy Living for Everyone
Regular exercise also produces changes in the circulation. Increased blood flow means that more oxygen and fuel can be delivered to the muscle cells.

1.1 Oxygen Cycle

Earth is the only known planet with life. Millions of species live on earth. These living organisms depend on each other in one or the other way. They also interact with their non-living environment. The study of interrelationship between organisms and their environment is called ecology.
1.1 Oxygen Cycle

Oxygen cycle plays an essential role in the existence of life on the earth. Few billion years ago there was no free molecular oxygen in the atmosphere. Today earth atmosphere has 21% oxygen which is largely product of photosynthesis carried out by plants. Plants use carbon dioxide to make food releasing oxygen as a byproduct.
1.1 Oxygen Cycle
Both animals and plants use oxygen in their respiration process to get energy.
1.2 Carbon Cycle

Carbon is constantly being removed from and released into the environment, in the form of carbon dioxide. The amount of carbon dioxide in atmosphere is 0.04%. Plants absorb this carbon dioxide to prepare their organic food by the process of photosynthesis. Animals gain carbon in the form of organic compounds when they feed on plants or other animals.
1.2 Carbon Cycle
The respiration process in both animals and plants releases carbon dioxide back to the environment.
1.2 Carbon Cycle

A chemical reaction between substances and oxygen in which CO₂, heat and light are produced, is called a combustion reaction. Animal and plant bodies buried under earth crust were converted into fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. The combustion of fossil fuels in factories, automobiles and houses is adding up carbon dioxide in the atmosphere rapidly.
1.2 Carbon Cycle

The oxygen cycle is interconnected with the carbon cycle. Oxygen is produced in photosynthesis and carbon dioxide is produced in respiration. Both these processes maintain the level of these gases in range to sustain life.
Stop and Check
A drastic change in the level of either of these gases represents a serious threat to life. What will happen if the level of carbon dioxide continues to increase?
1.3 Global Warming
The increase in average temperature of the earth is called global warming. The global temperature has been increased about 1 °C in the last 100 years.
Causes

Human population growth is a major contributor to global warming. Due to the increase in human population, the utilization of natural resources and the waste generated from the use of these resources has been increased massively. Excessive use of fossil fuels and deforestation are leading causes of global warming.
Causes
The burning of fossil fuels such as coal, gas and oil is adding carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is a leading greenhouse gas as it traps heat radiations.
Causes

Deforestation is the unplanned removal of trees on large scale which converts forest to non-forest land. Forests are removed to meet the increasing demand for land and materials. Major causes of deforestation are:
Causes
Urban development / urbanization • Infrastructure development like roads, rail tracks, air ports etc. • Timber and fibre requirement • Wood for fuel
Do you know?

Greenhouses are huge structures made mostly of glass or plastic sheets. Vegetables and fruits plants which cannot withstand cold can be grown in a greenhouse. Glass or plastic sheet traps heat energy to keep temperature higher than the surrounding environment.
Try it yourself
Visit a greenhouse near your home. • Measure the temperature outside and inside the greenhouse. • Name some plants growing inside the greenhouse.

1.4 Interactions in Ecosystem
In an ecosystem, living organisms interact with each other in different ways. Most common interactions are competition, predation and symbiosis.
Competition

Competition occurs when living organisms have to use common resources for their survival. Even members of the same species compete with each other for some resources. Animals compete for food, water and space to live. Plants compete for light, water, minerals and root space.
Predation

In predation, one organism attacks, actively kills and feeds on other organism. One which attacks and kills the other is called predator. Prey is the animal that is hunted and killed by predator for food.
Predation
Predator in one case can be prey in another case.
Predation
Some plants are also carnivorous. They prey upon insects and other small animals to fulfil their nitrogen deficiency e.g. pitcher plant and Venus fly trap.
Symbiosis
In symbiosis, members of two different species live together and at least one gets benefit from the other. Symbiosis has three types.
Parasitism
It is the association in which one member gets benefit and causes some harm to other member e.g. mosquito, liver fluke, leech and many types of bacteria.
Mutualism

You may have observed butterflies and honey bees in a flowered field of mustard. Can you name the interaction between insects and plants having brightly coloured flowers? Symbiotic interaction in which both members get benefit is called mutualism e.g. microorganisms in the gut of herbivores help to digest cellulose and get food and shelter in return.
Mutualism
Some bacteria live in intestine of man. They get food and provide us with some vitamins in return.
Commensalism

In this type of interaction one partner gets benefit without any benefit or harm to other organism, for example, a bird building nest on a tree, small plants (epiphytes) which grow on large trees for space to get better light.
Teaching Point
Teacher will discuss more examples of ecological interactions with students and their significance.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem

A system formed by the interaction of living organisms among each other and with their non-living environment is called ecosystem. The living organisms in any ecosystem are called producers, consumers and decomposers.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem
Producers have the ability to use light energy to produce food during photosynthesis. Plants and algae are producers of ecosystem.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem

Consumers are those which obtain energy by feeding on other organisms. All animals are consumers. Herbivores are primary consumers as they feed on green plants. Secondary and tertiary consumers feed on other animals so are carnivores.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem
Decomposers obtain energy by breaking down dead organisms and excretory products. Fungi and bacteria are examples of decomposers.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem
The feeding relationship between organisms can be represented in a food chain. A food chain is a series of organisms through which energy is transferred in the form of food.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem
However, in the ecosystem food chains are interlinked to form food web.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem

A lot of energy is lost to the environment as food is transferred from one level to the next in a food chain. Energy may be lost to the environment: as heat during respiration at each level; in uneaten body parts; through food material which remains undigested, and; through waste products excreted by consumers, for example urea.
1.5 Flow of Energy in an Ecosystem

More and more energy is lost as we go down a food chain. The total energy is highest at the producer level and lowest at the last level. The total energy in the various levels of a food chain can be represented in the form of a pyramid. This is called pyramid of energy. A pyramid of energy is always broad at the base and narrow toward the top.
Changes in water supply

Water is important for life. All forms of life directly depend on water availability. Aquatic life on earth is 90% of the total life on earth. Forests, wetlands and grasslands are critical part of the global water cycle. However, ecosystems are affected by floods and drought. Human impact on ecosystems has disturbed natural water cycles.
Changes in water supply
The wise use of water and treatment of sewage water can have positive effect on ecosystems.
Introduction of new population

Living organisms are adapted to their environment. Introduced species are new organisms brought into an ecological environment. If introduced species cannot adapt to new environment it will not survive. However, if that new species find a way to survive, it affects all the other species already living there. It may result in death of one or more native species.
Introduction of new population
With the passage of time ecosystem will reach a new equilibrium.
Hunting

Nature has a delicate balance and hunting by human can have impact on that natural balance. It is one of the causes of species extinction. If predators are hunted, their prey will increase in number. The decrease in the size of one population and increase in the other will change the ecosystem greatly.
Migration
Sometimes animals migrate from one area to another to get better food sources. Migration may alter the structure of already settled populations.
1.7 Positive Impact of Human on Ecosystem
A balanced ecosystem ensures that human beings have access to clean air, water and fertile land for agriculture. To save our planet and diverse ecosystems, a number of steps are being taken.
Reforestation

Reforestation is the plantation of trees where already existing forest has been destroyed by some cause. It is very important as trees decrease toxic gases from the surrounding nature. Forests are natural carbon sink. Planned forests can reduce global warming by decreasing greenhouse gases (mainly CO₂) from the air. Reforestation is a solution of stopping soil erosion to maintain land quality.
Reforestation
Forests support other plants and animal species, thus maintaining ecosystem.
Afforestation
Afforestation is plantation of forest on land where there was no forest before. It is very useful to increase forest land in Pakistan as we have very low forest coverage.
Control of Pollution
The addition of harmful substances in the environment is called pollution. The unjustified use of resources has damaged environment badly. Major pollution causing substances are:
Control of Pollution
Harmful gases and dust from factories • Pollutants from power stations and automobiles • Sewage from urban areas • Use of plastics
Control of Pollution
Air and water pollution has badly affected all forms of life. However, many steps are being taken to control pollution which will ultimately help to conserve endangered species.
Control of Air Pollution

The shift on clean energy sources will help reduce air pollution and reverse its effect on the environment. The use of wind power station and solar energy is replacing coal and oil power station. Electrical vehicles are becoming popular day by day.
Control of Water Pollution

Protection of clean water resources is a challenge. Water conservation, treatment of sewage from homes and industry, and less use of plastic are key steps to control water pollution. Thus, more clean water will be available to keep ecosystem flourishing.
Conservation of Endangered Species

Plants and animals maintain the health of an ecosystem. When a species becomes endangered, it is a sign that ecosystem is out of balance. Government, Non-governmental organization (NGOs), local communities and individuals work together to contribute towards growing the population of endangered species.
Conservation of Endangered Species
The awareness campaign aimed at getting more people involved in conservation work is very effective way for species conservation.

Teacher will discuss how balanced ecosystem is necessary for the survival of human and planet earth.

Key Points

• Green plants are producers which prepare food by photosynthesis. • Animals are consumers which depend on plants directly or indirectly. • Major portion of energy is lost in one to next level of food chain. • There is a need to take steps to conserve nature.

Unit 2: Human Nervous System

Various organs of human body play their role as and when required. These organs perform their duties in a precise way in harmony with each other. For example, heart rate and breathing increase during exercise to meet energy requirement of the muscles. However, organs cannot work properly by themselves. They require some signals for proper functioning.
Unit 2: Human Nervous System
Therefore, nervous system coordinates and regulates all the body functions.
2.1 Neuron
Nervous system is made up of cells called neurons. Neurons conduct messages in the form of electrical signals called nerve impulses.
Dendrites
Dendrites are fibres of neuron which transmit nerve impulses to the cell body.
Cell body
Cell body is the thick part of neuron which has nucleus and most of the cytoplasm.
Axon
Axon is the neuron fibre which transmits nerve impulses away from the cell body.
Types of Neurons
Neurons are of three types:
Types of Neurons

Sensory neurons transmit nerve impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. • Motor neurons transmit nerve impulses from the central nervous system to the effectors. • Interneurons are neurons of the central nervous system. They transmit nerve impulses from sensory neurons to the motor neurons.
Do you know?

Any change in environment which has some influence on living organism is called stimulus. • Sense organs or cells which receive stimulus are called receptors e.g., eyes, nose etc. • A muscle, gland or organ capable of responding to a stimulus is called effector. • The change in activity of the organism according to stimulus is called response.
2.2 Parts of Human Nervous System
Human body has very fast and precise method of communication in the form of nervous system. The human nervous system can be divided into two parts:
2.2 Parts of Human Nervous System

1. The central nervous system (CNS) consisting of the brain and the spinal cord. • 2. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) consisting of nerves which originate from brain (cranial nerves) and spinal cord (spinal nerves).
Working of Nervous System

Different stimuli are detected by receptor organs. This information is conveyed to central nervous system (CNS) through sensory neurons. The CNS analyses the stimulus and takes decision through motor neurons, CNS orders effectors to act accordingly.
Brain
Brain is protected in human skull. It is divided into three main parts i.e. forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.
Interesting Fact
The human brain is the most complex structure in the universe and it is far superior than any computer yet built.
Do you know?
The right cerebral hemisphere controls the left side of the body and the left hemisphere controls right side of the body.
Brain
Forebrain further consists of cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.
Brain

Cerebrum is the largest part of brain. Human cerebrum is the most advance in all animals. It is divided into right and left hemisphere. Cerebrum is the site of conscious (our sense of self), memory, intelligence, learning, reasoning, personality, emotions and will.
Brain
Thalamus plays critical role in the processing of perception. It receives sensory information from the receptor organs and sends them to the specific part of cerebrum.
Brain
Hypothalamus regulates body temperature, appetite, water balance and blood pressure. It has centres to control mood and emotions, such as aggression, anger, fear and pleasure.
Brain
Midbrain is reduced in human. It serves as a link between forebrain and hindbrain. It also controls the reflex movements of eye muscles.
Brain
Hindbrain consists of cerebellum, pons and medulla oblongata. Cerebellum is concerned with the control and precision of all movements involving voluntary muscles.
Brain

Pons is a bridge between cerebellum and other parts of brain. Medulla oblongata controls involuntary activities like heart rate, breathing rate, swallowing, vomiting, salivation, coughing and sneezing.
Note

Brain stem is the posterior part of the brain consisting of three parts i.e. mid brain, pons and medulla oblongata. It regulates most of body's automatic functions e.g. heart rate, breathing, blood pressure etc.
Stop and Check
What will happen if pleasure centre of a person is suppressed?
Spinal cord

Spinal cord is a cylinder of nervous tissue running from the base of the brain down to the back. It is protected by the backbone. Brain links to most of the body parts through spinal cord. Many reflex actions are controlled by the spinal cord e.g. withdrawal of hand on touching hot object.
Spinal cord

Spinal cord has a central butterfly shaped area called grey matter and outer to it is white matter. On the other hand, brain has outer grey matter and white matter to its centre. Grey matter has cell bodies of neuron and non-myelinated fibres. The white matter has myelinated fibres.
Peripheral nervous system

It is a system of nerves which link different body parts with the brain and spinal cord. A nerve contains many fibers of sensory neurons, motor neurons or both protected in a sheath of connective tissue.
Peripheral nervous system
Cranial nerves: These nerves originate from brain. Humans have 12 pairs of cranial nerves.
Peripheral nervous system
Spinal nerves: These nerves originate from spinal cord. There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves in humans.

Activities which are performed willingly are called voluntary actions. On the other hand involuntary actions are not under our conscious control.

3.1 Genetics

Since thousands of years humans understood that certain physical characteristics could be transmitted from one generation to another. Traits such as eye colour, skin colour, height and hair texture are passed from parents to offspring. Each individual has some features identical to parents, grandparents or siblings. Genetics is a field of biology that studies how traits are passed from parents to their offspring.
3.1 Genetics
The passing of traits to next generation is known as heredity, therefore, genetics is the study of heredity.
Stop and Check
Have you ever had such a fascinating experience that a stranger had recognized whose child you are or whose sibling you are? How was he able to make such an accurate guess? Share your experience.
3.2 Variations

Two individuals produced sexually are never genetically identical. Variations are differences in traits between individual of the same species. Variations within a species are essential for the survival of species.
3.2 Variations
In sexually reproducing organisms genetic variations are caused by:
3.2 Variations
Crossing over • Mutations
3.2 Variations
Environmental factors which cause variations include:
3.2 Variations
Diet • Temperature • Humidity
Types of Variations

Some variations have few distinct forms and are called discontinuous variations like free or attached ear lobes and blood groups. On the other hand the variations which have a wide range of types from one extreme to other are called continuos variations e.g. human height and skin colour.
3.3 Adaptation

Adaptation is the mechanism by which a species becomes fit to its environment. Individuals of a species may differ in many traits. Some may be larger, hairier, fight off infections better, or have smaller ears. Some of these traits provide competitive advantages like speed, strength, or attractiveness. More adaptive characters mean better survival rates.
3.3 Adaptation
So well-adapted organisms live longer, get chance to produce more offspring and the species as a whole becomes successful.
3.3 Adaptation
An adaptation can be structural, meaning it is a physical part of the organism. An adaptation can also be behavioral, affecting the way an organism responds to its environment.
3.3 Adaptation
An example of a structural adaptation is the way some plants have adapted to life in dry and hot deserts. Such plants store water in their short, thick stems or leaves e.g. cactus.
3.3 Adaptation

Seasonal migration is an example of a behavioural adaptation. Many birds migrate from Siberia to Pakistan and some other countries to avoid extreme cold. Similarly many plants shed their leaves in winter to prevent water loss.
Try it yourself
Watch few videos of cheetah hunting on some other animal. Enlist structural adaptations which make cheetah a good predator.
3.4 Chromosomes and DNA

Life depends on the ability of cell to store and transfer its genetic information to the next generation. This ability of the cell resides in its nucleus as it has chromosomes. Each kind of organism has a specific number of chromosomes. The chromosomes occur in pairs. Humans have 46 chromosomes in all body cells. Chromosomes are made up of proteins and DNA. Proteins fold and pack DNA in the chromosome.
3.4 Chromosomes and DNA
DNA is responsible for the transmission of hereditary information from one generation to the next.
3.4 Chromosomes and DNA
DNA on the chromosomes forms genes. Genes control traits of organisms like skin colour, height, blood groups in human. Chromosomes carry these genes to next generations when cells divide.
Chemical composition of DNA
DNA is the hereditary material of all the living organisms. It is made up of small units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of three components. These are:
Chemical composition of DNA
5-carbon sugar called deoxyribose • Phosphate group • Nitrogen containing bases
Chemical composition of DNA
There are four types of nitrogenous bases: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, Thymine.
Chemical composition of DNA
The type of nucleotide depends on the type of nitrogenous base. So there are four types of nucleotides which depend on the type of nitrogenous base.
Chemical composition of DNA

Many nucleotides join in a specific order to form a polynucleotide strand. Two polynucleotide strands are coiled around each other in manner of a spiral ladder to form DNA molecule. In a DNA molecule, adenine in one strand forms a link with thymine in the opposite strand. Similarly, guanine pairs with cytosine.

3.5 Cell Division

The life of each sexually produced organism starts from a single cell called zygote. The continuous process of cell division produces huge number of cells which change into different types to form tissues and organs of the organism. An adult human body has trillions of cells which are all produced from zygote by the process of cell division. Cell division has two types: mitosis and meiosis.
3.6 Mitosis

In mitosis a parent cell divides to produce two identical daughter cells. Both daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes as in the parent cell. Growth, development, healing of wounds, regeneration and asexual reproduction take place through mitosis. Before the start of mitosis, cell replicates its entire DNA so as to produce an extra copy of each chromosome.
3.6 Mitosis
At first, the nucleus divides into two nuclei, and then cytokinesis takes place.
3.6 Mitosis
The division of the nucleus takes place in four phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
3.6 Mitosis
Before the start of cell division, cell replicates its DNA. So cell contains two copies of its entire DNA one for each daughter cell.
3.6 Mitosis

Prophase: DNA is coiled up tightly so chromosomes become visible. As DNA is already replicated, each chromosome has two chromatids attached at centromere. Nuclear membrane disappears and spindle fibres begin to form.
3.6 Mitosis
Metaphase: All chromosomes are aligned in the centre of the cell and are attached themselves to the spindle fibres by their centromeres.
3.6 Mitosis
Anaphase: Each centromere splits. The separated chromatids are pulled to the opposite poles of the cell.
3.6 Mitosis
Telophase: Chromosomes uncoil, become long and thin. Nuclear membrane reappears around the chromosomes, forming two new nuclei.
3.6 Mitosis
Cytokinesis: In cytokinesis, cytoplasm divides and the two newly formed daughter cells separate from each other.
3.7 Meiosis

Meiosis takes place to produce reproductive cells called gametes i.e. eggs and sperms. For sexually reproducing organisms, zygote is formed by the fusion of a sperm with an egg. This means egg and sperm must have half the number of chromosomes as compare to the normal body cell. Meiosis is a reduction division which reduces number of chromosomes to half in gametes.
3.7 Meiosis
Moreover a process called crossing over helps to create variations in the next generations.
3.7 Meiosis
It involves two consecutive divisions; meiosis I and meiosis II. As a result four daughter cells are produced each having half the number of chromosomes as compared to parent cell.
Meiosis I

Prophase I: Chromosomes appear as thick threads due to tight coiling of DNA. As there are two chromosomes of each type, identical chromosomes pair with each other. These chromosomes exchange segments. This process is called crossing over which results in variations in offspring.
Meiosis I
…irs of chromosomes arrange themselves in the centre of the cell.
Meiosis I
Anaphase I: Paired chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles. Each pole receives one member of all chromosomal pairs i.e. half chromosomes compared to parental cell.
Meiosis I
Telophase I: Nuclear membrane is formed around the chromosomes at each pole. Thus, two daughter cells with half chromosomes are formed each of which divides again by meiosis II.
Meiosis II
Two daughter cells formed after meiosis I divide again. This process of meiosis II is just like mitosis.
Meiosis II
Finally four daughter cells are produced each having half the number of chromosomes as compared to parent cell.

Unit 5: The Periodic Table

Recall that the atomic number of an element is the number of protons in the nucleus of atom of an element. Each element has a different atomic number. The elements also have different number of electrons. These electrons are arranged in energy levels called shells. Electrons present in the outermost shell are called valence electrons. These electrons take part in chemical reactions.
Unit 5: The Periodic Table

If you have a large number of books in your study room and place them in a haphazard way, it will be very difficult to find the book you need. However, if these books are arranged into groups according to some common features, it would become easier to find the book you are looking for.
5.1 Introduction

Location of Elements in the Periodic Table:

Location of an element in the periodic table largely depends on its electrons. • The total number of valence shell electrons determine its group and the number of valence shell in which electrons lie determines the period number.
Steps:

1. Write distribution of electrons in shells. • 2. Note the n value of the valence shell, this indicates period number. n=1 for K shell, n=2 for L shell, n=3 for M shell • 3. Count total number of electrons in the valence shell. This indicates group number. • 4. Remember K shell contains maximum 2 electrons, L shell contains 8 electrons and M can hold maximum 18 electrons.
Identifying the location of carbon (atomic number 6) in the periodic table.
Solution: Electron distribution in carbon: C = 2, 4.
1. Valence shell is L, its n value is 2, so carbon is present in second period. • 2. Total number of valence electrons = 4 so its group is IVA in the periodic table.
Identifying the location of magnesium (atomic number 12) in the periodic table.

1. Electron distribution in magnesium: Mg = 2, 8, 2 • 2. As valence shell is M, n = 3. So, Mg is present in the third period. • 3. Total number of valence electrons is 2, so Mg belongs to IIA in the periodic table.
Identifying the location of Chlorine (atomic number 17) in the periodic table.

1. Electron distribution in Chlorine: Cl = 2, 8, 7 • 1. As valence shell is M, n = 3. So, Cl is present in the third period. • 2. Total number of valence electrons is 7, so Cl belongs to VIIA in the periodic table.

6.3 Law of Conservation of Mass

A balanced chemical equation is based on the principle that atoms are neither created nor lost in a chemical reaction. So total mass of reactants and products is conserved. This principle is called law of conservation of mass.
6.3 Law of Conservation of Mass
The law of conservation of mass states that the total mass of all the products of a chemical reaction is equal to the total mass of all the reactants.

Chemical Bonds

Atoms combine to form various types of substances. What holds them together in a substance? Fundamentally, some forces of attraction hold atoms together in substances. These forces are called chemical bonds. Electronic structure of an atom helps us to understand how atoms are held together in a substance. Atoms of noble gases have no tendency to react with other atoms of elements.
Chemical Bonds

The atoms of noble gases already have complete valence shells. Helium contains 2 electrons in valence K shell. Other noble atoms have 8 electrons in their valence shell. So, they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons. Atoms other than noble gases have a tendency to react with the atoms of other elements. This is because they do not have complete valence shells.
Chemical Bonds
They tend to gain, lose or share electrons to acquire the electronic configuration of next noble gas.
Types of Bonds
Depending on the tendency of an atom to lose or gain or share electrons, there are two types of bonds.
Types of Bonds
1. Ionic bonds • 2. Covalent bonds
Ionic Bond:

Ionic bonds are formed between two atoms when an atom loses electron(s) to form cation and the other gains this, to form anion. Cations and anions have opposite charges. They attract one another by electrostatic forces (non-contact forces).
Ionic Bond:
The force of attraction that binds oppositely charged ions is called Ionic bond.
Ionic Bond:

Compounds that consist of ions joined together by electrostatic forces are called ionic compounds. Ionic bonds are found in compounds that contain metals combined with non-metals. Recall that metal atoms form cations and non-metal atoms form anions. In the formation of ionic bond, electrons are transferred from the metal atoms to the non-metal atoms during the chemical reaction.
Ionic Bond:
What happens when sodium and chlorine combine to make sodium chloride (NaCl)?
Ionic Bond:

Sodium atom has only one electron in its outermost or valence shell. Chlorine has 7 electrons in its valence shell. It needs only one electron to complete its valence shell. When these two elements react, the outer electron of sodium atom is transferred to the outer shell of chlorine atom. After losing one electron sodium atom has become sodium ion (Na⁺). Its remaining outermost shell has eight electrons.
Ionic Bond:

After gaining one electron chlorine atom has become chloride ion (Cl⁻). Its outermost shell also has eight electrons. In this way both the atoms acquire nearest noble gas electronic configuration. These oppositely charged ions are pulled to one another by strong electrostatic forces. This type of bonding is called ionic bonding.
Ionic Bond:
We can represent the formation of ionic bond between sodium and chlorine atoms by using electron-dot and electron-cross structures.

Covalent Bond:
The bond formed by mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms is called covalent bond.
Covalent Bond:
Consider the formation of covalent bond in hydrogen molecule. A hydrogen atom has a single valence electron. Two hydrogen atoms share their valence electrons to form a diatomic molecule.
Covalent Bond:

In the formation of this molecule, each hydrogen atom attains the electron configuration of the noble gas helium, which has two valence electrons. An electron pair in the region between the two atoms, is attracted to both hydrogen nuclei. This means it is a more stable situation than that exists in separate atoms. Because of this stability, two atoms form a covalent bond.
Covalent Bond:

We can represent the formation of a covalent bond between two atoms using electron-dot and electron-cross symbols for the atoms and the resulting molecule. A shared pair of electrons is also represented by a dash (-) in a molecule.
Covalent Bond:
Covalent bond is formed by the sharing of one electron pair is called single covalent bond. So, hydrogen molecule contain a single covalent bond.
Covalent Bond:

Sometimes atoms may share two or three electron pairs to complete their valence shell. Double covalent bonds are the bonds that are formed by sharing of two electron pairs between two atoms. Triple covalent bonds are the bonds that involve three shared electrons pairs between two atoms.
Covalent Bond:

Consider the formation of O₂ molecule. Oxygen is in Group VI A, so it has 6 electrons in the valence shell. It needs two electrons to complete its valence shell. So for sharing each O-atom contributes two electrons

Key Points

A chemical change is called a chemical reaction. • Burning is a chemical change. • Colour change, emission of a gas, formation of precipitate, odour and temperature change are signs that indicate a chemical reaction has taken place. • During chemical reaction the arrangement of atoms changes due to formation of new bonds between atoms. • The chemical equation is the symbolic representation of a chemical reaction.
Key Points

• While balancing a chemical equation, do not change the chemical formulae. • Law of conservation of mass states that the total mass of reactants and products is conserved. • In a synthesis reaction, two or more reactants combine to form a single product. • In a decomposition reaction one reactant produces two or more products.
Key Points

• In a displacement reaction a more reactive element takes the place of less reactive element. • In a double displacement reaction two atoms or group of atoms exchange their places. • Heat is evolved in an exothermic reaction. • Heat is absorbed evolved in an endothermic reaction. • The force of attraction that binds oppositely charged ions is called ionic bond.
Key Points

• The bond formed by mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms is called covalent bond. • Covalent bonds formed by the sharing of one, two and three electron pairs are called single, double and triple covalent bonds respectively.

7.1 Introduction to Acids, Bases and Salts

Acids

Many fruits such as lemon, orange, grapes, etc. taste sour. What makes them sour? There must be a substance in these fruits that makes them sour. This substance is called an acid. The word acid is derived from Latin word "acidus" meaning sour.
Acids

An acid is a substance that contains a hydrogen atom bonded, which ionizes in aqueous solution to produce hydrogen (H⁺) ions. This hydrogen ion makes acid taste sour. So an acid is defined as follows.
Acids
An acid is a substance that gives hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water.
Acids
Hydrochloric acid (HCl) contains one ionizable hydrogen. How many ionizable hydrogen are present in sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)?
Acids

HCl, H₂SO₄ and carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) are derived from minerals and are called mineral acids. The acids present in animals and plants materials are known as organic acids. For instance, acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is obtained from vinegar, formic acid (HCOOH) is present in bee sting etc.
Acids

Acids are also classified on the basis of ionizing capacity. Acids that ionize in water completely are called strong acids. For example: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃ etc. Acids that ionize in water partially are called weak acids. For example: Vinegar, formic acid, carbonic acid etc.
Acids

Bases

What happens when soap lather gets into your eyes? Which substance produces irritation and burning in eyes? Soaps, detergents and shampoos have bitter taste. Which substance makes them bitter? This substance is called a base. Bases contain hydroxyl group (OH), which dissociates or ionizes in aqueous solution to produce hydroxide ions. These hydroxide ions make bases taste bitter.
Bases

A compound that has a bitter taste is called a base. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali. Like acids, alkalies are very common substances which are found in home and industry. The word alkali is derived from Arabic word "qali" meaning from "ashes". Alkalies were first obtained from ashes of plants.
Bases
Alkalies are the compounds that produce hydroxide ions (OH⁻) when dissolved in water. For example, sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, etc.
Bases

Alkalies are also classified on the basis of ionizing capacity. Alkalies that ionize in water completely are called strong alkalies. For example: NaOH, KOH. Alkalies that ionize in water partially are called weak alkalies. For example: NH₄OH, Cu(OH)₂ etc.

Salts
What are the main products formed when acids react with alkalies? We can write a general word equation for this reaction.
Salts

The word salt is used to describe a group of compounds formed from acids. All simple acids contain one or more replaceable hydrogen. When such a hydrogen is replaced by a metal, the resulting compound is called a salt. For example when hydrogen from hydrochloric acid is replaced by sodium, the resulting compound sodium chloride (NaCl) is a salt. Sodium sulphate Na₂SO₄ is produced from sulphuric acid.
Salts
Which acid forms nitrates?
Salts

Normal salts: A salt that does not contain any replaceable hydrogen atom or hydroxyl group is called normal salt. They are formed by complete neutralization of acid and base. Examples: NaCl, Na₂SO₄, CaSO₄, KCl etc.
Salts
Acid salts: A salt that contains replaceable hydrogen atoms is called an acid salt. Examples: NaHCO₃, NaHSO₄ etc.
Salts
Basic salts: A salt that contains replaceable hydroxyl group is called basic salt. Examples: Zn(OH)Cl, Pb(OH)Cl
Salts
Double salt: A salt that contains two different cations or anions is called double salt. Examples: Dolomite CaCO₃·MgCO₃, Alum K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O

Indicators: The easiest way to detect an acid or an alkali is to use an indicator. Indicators are substances that change colour when added to an acid or alkali. The most common indicator is litmus. It turns red in an acid and turns blue in an alkali.
