1. Turnitin is web-based plagiarism prevention system. • 2. A "text-matching" software which is designed to educate students regarding appropriate citation and referencing techniques. • 3. Empower students to do their best, original work.
5.1.7 Digital Piracy

Digital piracy means illegally copying digital content in any form without the consent of the owner. Digital piracy is also known as Internet piracy and online piracy. Some examples of digital piracy are unlawfully copying or downloading copyrighted music, movie, computer software, game or electronic book without the consent of the owner. Digital piracy is a crime as it is violation of owner's copyright.
5.1.7 Digital Piracy
There are some websites that make digital content available for free download.
5.2 Cybercrime

Cybercrime refers to any crime that is committed by means of computer and Internet technology by having unlawful access to others' computers. Unfortunately, the computer technology is also used by criminals to harm the society. Cybercrime is growing day by day and it is a serious concern for governments all over the world.
5.2 Cybercrime
Commonly committed cybercrimes include:
5.2 Cybercrime

Stealing personal information of people such as username, password, credit card number etc. for committing various types of crimes. • Downloading illegal software, music files and videos. • Committing fraud, kidnapping, murder etc. with the use of computer. • Internet harassment or cyber bullying. • Sending threatening email, spreading rumors or virus and posting negative comments about people.
5.2.1 Hacker

A person who illegally breaks into others' computer systems is known as hacker. Hackers have in-depth knowledge of digital technology. Hacking is a cybercrime. Hackers gain unauthorized access to computer systems for stealing or changing information or to get credit card or bank account details for financial benefits.
5.2.2 Internet and Privacy

People who use Internet are worried about privacy of their personal information. Internet users enter their personal information in websites to sign up or register for services without realizing that this may lead to invasion of privacy. This information can be accessed by hackers and used for harmful purpose. This poses a serious threat to privacy.
5.2.2 Internet and Privacy
It is the responsibility of organizations by law not to allow unauthorized people to have access to personal information or disclose it to anyone outside the organization.
5.3 Malware

Malware means malicious software. It includes a number of harmful software that are threat to all the computer users. Malware is created for attack on privacy, spying, destruction and financial benefits.
Do you know?
Computer virus and biological virus are very different from each other. Computer virus does not harm living things.
Computer viruses

A computer virus is a type of malware that spreads by inserting a copy of itself into another program or file. It infects other files when a computer user opens the infected program or file. It spreads to other computers through network, USB flash drive, and infected emails. Computer viruses can seriously damage the computer hardware as well.
Worms

A worm is a malware that transmits itself over a network to infect other computers. It is also harmful like a computer virus. It spreads automatically in computer networks and replicates itself. Most of the worms cause some harm to the network. They can also slow down the network communication.
Spyware

Spyware is a program developed to spy on computer users by gathering information about their activities on the computer. It is used for stealing password, banking PIN (Personal Identification Number) or other personal information about user. It infects computer during installation of software from the Internet.
Adware

Adware is a malware that attaches itself to free software on the Internet and infects computer when such software is downloaded. It pops up advertisements during execution of infected program. Some adware may collect user information without their permission.
Common Symptoms of Malware Attacks

The computer does not start. • Computer reboots automatically. • Different messages appear on the screen. • Programs do not run properly. • Computer runs slow. • Folders or files are deleted. • Web browser does not run in a normal way.
Tip
Enable Windows Defender to protect your computer from malware if you don't have anti-virus software installed.
5.3.2 Protecting Computer from Malware

We have to install antivirus or anti-spyware software to safeguard against malware. Antivirus software is a computer program that detects and removes viruses and other types of malware. Anti-spyware is also a program that detects spyware and removes it. It helps to protect computer against security threats caused by spyware and other types of malware.
5.4 Major Uses of Internet

Internet is the global network. It has become a vital part of our daily life. It is used in all the fields. These include business, banks, entertainment, government sector, education, e-commerce, hospitals. Following are some major uses of Internet.
Use of Internet in Business

It helps in marketing and advertisement of brands. • Allows communication and web conferencing with customers and suppliers. • Helps to do survey and testing on product sale and online services. • Builds business and customer relationships. • Helps business to sell products and services online. • Help businesses perform various tasks on daily basis.
Use of Internet in Social Networking

Helps people to stay connected with family and friends. • Helps to connect people and businesses. • Helps businesses to do marketing, advertisement and buy/sale of products. • Helps in organizing activities and events. • Helps people to exchange views/ideas and work and think together. • Allows people to participate in discussions. • Helps people to share their creative work such as writing, music, photography, etc.
Use of Internet in Entertainment

Users can watch live sports. • Users can watch shows and movies. • Users can play online games with friends. • Users enjoy chatting with friends. • Users can listen to Internet radio and television. • YouTube allows user to upload videos on servers and share with other users all over the world. • Users can easily have access to jokes, poems or magazines for free.
Use of Internet for News and Information

Internet is the major source of news and information for people all over the world. • Access to Internet for news and information is just a click away. • Computer users can use search engines such as google and yahoo to easily find any information about anything. • Internet helps researchers to find information on any topic for preparing their projects.
Use of Internet in Education

Social media and messaging apps help teachers and students to remain intact. • Teachers can share study material like quiz and lessons with their students. • Students can share new idea with fellow classmates and enrich their knowledge. • Internet provides education through web tutorials and videos. • Internet keeps the students up to date with the latest information on any subject.
5.5 Digital Media Bias

Digital Media Bias is the perception that media is reporting the news in a prejudiced manner. It is inclination, prejudice or tendency towards or against a person, group, idea or belief. It is unjust favoritism of journalists in reporting various events, ideas and stories. Media bias occurs when media favors a specific viewpoint.
5.5 Digital Media Bias

Media bias can also occur when journalists are influenced by personal feelings or opinions. It is almost impossible to be completely unbiased as it is natural human instinct to make biased judgements. There are a number of international watchdogs that report on bias media.
5.6 Positive and Negative Impact of Social Media
Social media has both positive and negative impact.
5.6.1 Positive Impact

Helps to remain connected with family and friends. • Fast communication increases the impact of events around the world. • Helps in spreading social awareness. • Provides a platform to share ideas and creative work. • Helps students to form study groups. • Helps people learn new skills. • Provides entertainment. • Helps in building businesses. • Makes it easy to make friends.
5.6.2 Negative Impact

Easy to spread false information. • Reduces face-to-face contact with people. • Social media addiction can affect mental and physical health. • People can commit fraud and scam through online networking. • Arguments over social media may cause stress. • People can bully each other online.

5.8 Who is a Cyber Scout

Cyber Scout is a person with unique aim to promote awareness about cybercrime in the society. A cyber Scout is trained to identify cyber crime activities, and equipped with adequate preventive knowledge to help fight this menace. He understands the risks associated with virtual socializing and works to promote cyber safety in his surrounding environment.
5.8 Who is a Cyber Scout
A cyber Scout plays a vital role to create cyber awareness among fellow students, teachers and parents.

6.1 Business Plan
Business Plan is a formal written document that describes the company's goals, strategy and implementation for the growth of an organization.
6.1 Business Plan
A detailed business plan template provides guidance to establishing your company mission, customer research, competition, and a business strategy to profitability.
6.1 Business Plan

To start a successful business, we must conduct an analysis and research the market first. Market research will tell about the opportunity to turn your idea into a successful business. After that, write your business plan which demonstrates that how much money and time is required to start a new project. If a business plan is compelling enough, it can also convince investors to give you funding.
Tip
Business planning isn't a one-off-event, it should be an ongoing practice of self assessment and planning.
6.2.1 Customer Needs

Customer needs analysis is the process of identifying the requirements of the customers about a product or service. The goal of a customer need analysis survey is to understand the market gap for a new product to launch and penetrate the existing market. The market analysis provides a clear picture of the product demand and provides the evidence that your company can exploit in an effective manner.
6.2.1 Customer Needs
This analysis provides the foundation on which your marketing plan will execute and identifies your competitors, their strengths and weaknesses.
6.2.2 Product Design

Product design is the process that involves steps to launch a successful product based on user requirements and ultimately acquires customer satisfaction, theoretically. The key to successful product design is to understand the exact requirement of the end-user for whom the product is being designed. It is very important to design the interface of the product as attractive as possible which increases its usage.
6.2.3 Costing

A business plan includes the set-up estimated cost like legal cost, attorney fees and license fee etc. The plan should also includes funding to cover the other expenses, revenue collected against sale and profit or loss.
6.2.4 Operations

The operations includes the objectives, goals, procedures, and timeline of your organization. An operation plan assists the businessman to meet the deadlines. For example, if a manufacturer develops a plan to expand revenue by 60% that plan will include a marketing, sales and operations component.
6.2.4 Operations
The operations component of the plan would include procurement, manufacturing and logistics strategies that enable the firm to boost production to support revenue growth.

6.2.5 Marketing

It is the action or business of promoting and selling products or services, including market research and advertising. The following are the four elements of marketing: product, price, promotion, and place.
Product
A product (goods and services) is a main entity which your business offers to the end user. What makes your product to be purchased versus the products offered by the competitors?
Price
Price is an important element to decide keeping in mind the competitive price of the product. For example, is a cheaper product always less in quality?
Promotion

This includes the packaging and position/place of the product or service in the marketplace, where customers can be attracted. The marketing tools are used to promote the sales of a particular product or service.
Place
The success of the business also based on the location of the outlet and the mode of sell either by e-commerce or telephone or will your product be carried in retail outlets?
6.3 Value Proposition

A value proposition refers an innovation or service intended to make a product attractive for customers. A value proposition helps customers truly understand the value of your company's products and services. It is a business or marketing statement that a company uses to summarize why a consumer should buy a product or use a service.
6.4 Promotion

Promotion refers to the awareness of a product or service to increase sales. The key objective of Promotion is to draw the attention of end users and to encourage them to make immediate purchase of the product or service.
6.4 Promotion
Example: "Buy 1 Get 1 free" offer, draws the attention of the customers.
6.5 Quality Assurance
Quality is all about meeting the needs and expectations of customers with respect to functionality, design, reliability, durability and price of the product.
6.5 Quality Assurance
Assurance is a positive declaration on a product or service which gives confidence to the user.

6.5 Quality Assurance

Quality Assurance is a procedure to ensure the quality of products or services provided to the customers by an organization. Quality assurance focuses on improving the development process and making it efficient and effective as per the quality standards defined for products.
6.5 Quality Assurance
Quality assurance helps a company to design and create the product which meets the expectations of customers. It produces high quality product that builds up the trust and loyalty of the customers.

Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is the process of improving your website to increase its visibility when people search for products or services related to your business in Google, Bing and other search engines.

An enabler is a leader who gives confidence and strength to their team and facilitates them to complete their tasks in a positive context.
6.7 Technology as an Enabler
Technology Enablers include governments, regulatory bodies and other organizations that facilitate technology adoption through standards, guidelines, policies, funding and investment.
6.8 Digital platform
Digital platform is an electronic tool for communication that includes mobile, social and email software. This covers websites and Social Media like Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, Amazon etc.
6.8 Digital platform
A Digital Business Platform (DBP) is a multi-purpose hub that helps an organization to coordinate work and supports business interactions between human beings and technology.
6.9 Transaction
A transaction is an agreement between a buyer and a seller to exchange goods, services or financial assets in return for money.
6.10 Payment
Payment is the transfer of money against the purchase of goods or services. Payment is the act of paying while the transaction is the act of conducting or carrying out business.
Do you know?
Google is the leading digital platform and shares 37% of ads worldwide.
6.10.1 Methods of payment
Following are the most commonly used methods of payment.
Credit cards

Credit cards are still considered as the most secure and safe method of online payment. Credit cards use online security features like encryption and fraud monitoring to keep your accounts and personal information safe. The transaction is regulated by payments compliance standards, such as the 3D secure flows.
Debit cards
Debit card is an efficient and simple form of payment. Unlike credit cards, debit cards don't allow you to overspend. You can withdraw cash at your local bank or at an ATM using a debit card.
Inter Bank transfer
Bank transfer (or wire transfer) is a payment method that allows consumers to transfer money to a bank account around the world. Bank transfer is also a very safe and secure payment method.
Mobile payment
Mobile payment is a convenient method of payment nowadays. In this method you can transfer money through your mobile and get cash on any commercial outlet.

Digital marketing is primarily data-driven as compared to traditional marketing methods such as print, billboards, and TV.

Unit 1: Oceans and Seas
Surface of the Earth has been covered with large landmasses and vast water bodies. Landmasses are known as continents and vast water bodies are identified as oceans and seas.
Unit 1: Oceans and Seas

Water covers about 71 % of total surface area of the Earth. Position of the different continents has subdivided the water covered area into five oceans. Oceans are huge bodies of saltwater surrounding the continents. Seas are water bodies smaller than oceans.
Unit 1: Oceans and Seas

Seas are partially enclosed margins of the oceans; a large landlocked lake can also be termed as a sea. Almost all the oceans have a number of seas along their coast lines, yet there are large water bodies found in the interiors of the continents that are termed as seas.
1.1 Origin of Oceans and Seas

Earth processes that formed the ocean beds stretch over long period of time. These processes involved the movement of tectonic plates. A brief history of formation of the ocean beds has been explained here.
1.1 Origin of Oceans and Seas

A supercontinent, known as Rodina existed about 600 million years ago. It split apart and oceans filled the basins. Tectonic plates collided, thrusting up mountain ranges. A new polar supercontinent, Pannotia, formed.
1.1 Origin of Oceans and Seas

A breakaway portion of Pannotia drifted north about 500 million years ago, splitting into three masses—Laurentia (North America), Baltica (Northern Europe), and Siberia. In shallow waters, the first multicellular animals with exoskeletons appeared, and the Cambrian explosion of life took off. 300 million years ago Laurentia collided with Baltica and later with Avalonia (Britain and New England).
1.1 Origin of Oceans and Seas
The Appalachian Mountains arose along the edge of the supercontinent, Pangea.
1.1 Origin of Oceans and Seas

Dinosaurs roamed Pangea about 200 million years ago, that stretched nearly from pole to pole and almost encircled Tethys, the oceanic ancestor of the Mediterranean Sea. The immense Panthalassic Ocean surrounded the supercontinent.
1.1 Origin of Oceans and Seas
About 100 million years ago Pangea broke apart. The Atlantic poured in between Africa and the Americas. India split away from Africa, and Antarctica and Australia were stranded near the South Pole.

1.6 Movements of Oceans
Ocean water remains under different types of motions due to the influence of different types of forces. These movements can be classified as waves, tides or currents.
i) Waves

Waves are series of crests and troughs that are developed on the surface of water by dragging effects of winds. Waves do not displace water from one place to another, rather they are the means of moving energy through water.
i) Waves

There are several types of waves such as ripples, chops, swells and tsunamis. Ripples are smallest waves and chops are a collection of small waves that make the ocean surface rough. Swells are deep water waves, that travel great distances whereas tsunami is a set of waves created by an earthquake.
ii) Tides

Periodical rise and fall of the sea level due to the force of attraction of the Moon and the Sun is called tides. Sea level rises and falls twice in a day. This rise of sea level is termed as high tide and fall in sea level is termed as low tide. Shores of continents and islands facing the Moon and those which are opposite to it, experience high tides.
ii) Tides
Shores of continents and islands that are neither facing the Moon nor are opposite to it experience low tides.
ii) Tides
There are two types of tides with reference to relative positions of the Sun, Moon and Earth.
a. Spring tides

When the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line, high tides rise to higher levels and low tides fall to lower level than normal. These higher high tides and lower low tides are called spring tides and they occur on the occasions of Full and New Moon.
b. Neap tides

When the Sun and Moon are at right angles with respect to the Earth, high tides do not rise so high and low tides do not fall so low. Such moderate tides are known as neap tides and they occur on 7th and 21st day of the Moon.

iii) Currents

Ocean currents are continuous, directed movement of ocean water caused by a number of factors. Ocean currents have specific names, directions, and speed. Ocean Currents can be grouped into surface and deep currents. Surface Currents are caused by winds and their direction is modified by effects of rotation of the Earth and continental margins.
iii) Currents
Whereas deep currents are caused by salinity and temperature differences of the water.
iii) Currents

Surface currents are of two types, i.e., cold currents and warm currents. Cold currents flow from polar to equatorial areas. These currents move along the western coasts of the continents for example the California and Peru currents.
iii) Currents
Warm Currents move from equatorial to the polar areas. These currents move along the eastern margins of the continents for example the Gulf Stream and Brazil current.
iii) Currents
Since the Pacific and Atlantic oceans are the largest oceans of the world, their major currents are briefly described below.
a. Currents of the Pacific Ocean
There are two circular loops of ocean currents in Pacific Ocean. These loops are called gyres. In Northern Pacific, currents move clockwise and in Southern Pacific, currents move anti-clockwise.
a. Currents of the Pacific Ocean

The great circular loop of the Northern Pacific is formed by four currents. These are North Equatorial Current, Kuroshio or Japan Current, North Pacific Current and Californian Current. Californian Current and Oyashio Currents are also cold currents that moves towards this loop from the north.
a. Currents of the Pacific Ocean

In South Pacific circular pattern of currents is completed by South Equatorial Current, East Australia Current, West Wind Drift and the Peruvian Current. West Wind Drift and the Peruvian current are cold currents of the South Pacific.

b. Currents of the Atlantic Ocean

Like the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean also has two large loops of currents. Loop of the Northern Atlantic consists of North Equatorial Current, Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, and Canary Current. Canary Current is a cold current that brings cold polar water to the equatorial region.
b. Currents of the Atlantic Ocean
There are two more cold currents, i.e., East Greenland and Labrador. These currents move southward from the east and west of the Greenland landmass.
b. Currents of the Atlantic Ocean

In the South Atlantic Ocean, the circulation of currents in the loop is anticlockwise. The loop is completed by the South Equatorial Current, Brazil Current, West Wind Drift and Benguela Current. West Wind Drift and Benguela are cold currents.

1.7 Role of Marine Biodiversity in our Environment

Marine biodiversity represents the variety of life in the ocean and seas. It has significant role in healthy functioning of our planet as it provides oxygen and absorbs carbon dioxide. It strengthen the prosperity, health and well-being of humanity.

1.7 Role of Marine Biodiversity in our Environment
Marine biodiversity plays a very important role in shaping and maintaining our physical environment in the following ways:
1.7 Role of Marine Biodiversity in our Environment

(i) Marine plants supply about 50% of the oxygen to the atmosphere. About 26% of the carbon dioxide emitted through human activities is absorbed by the them. • (ii) The amount of energy produced per unit area by plants in one year is called primary productivity. Half of the world's Net Primary Productivity comes from marine plants. These plants serve as the basic food for all types of oceanic life.
1.7 Role of Marine Biodiversity in our Environment

Smaller marine animals that consume these plants become a source of food for larger marine animals. • (iii) Fishing provides high quality protein fish and fishery products provide food security to hundreds of millions of people. • (iv) Marine plants such as kelp and seagrass, together with reefs provide habitats for many marine life forms, such as shrimp, fish and molluscs.
1.7 Role of Marine Biodiversity in our Environment
• (v) Gastropods (marine snails and slugs) and shrimps, that feed on micro-algae eventually become food for larger crabs, lobsters and fish.

Unit 2: Living with the Climate

Climate refers to the average weather conditions of a place over a long period of time. Usually, 30-35 years averages of weather conditions are taken as benchmark to declare the state of climate of a place. Weather is the state of the atmosphere of a place, at a given time. It refers to the conditions of the atmosphere at a specific place over a short period of time.
2.1 Extreme Weather on the Earth

Deviation from regular weather patterns leads to extreme weather or extreme climate. These events include unexpected, unusual, severe, or unseasonal weather. Extreme weather is a deviation of weather in terms of intensity from the range that has been seen in the past.
Hurricanes

Hurricanes are a type of extreme weather. Hurricanes are giant, spiraling tropical cyclones. They include strong winds of over 252 kilometers per hour. They produce heavy rains. They are caused by intense heating of sea surfaces, strong convective uplift of air and high moisture content in air.
Do you know
The Saffir–Simpson scale classifies Hurricanes by wind speed. Hurricane Katrina that devastated the city of New Orleans reached to Category 5.

Flood

Flooding happens when there is heavy rainfall in a short time. River waters flow beyond the natural or artificial levees onto the land in either side of the natural levees. Flooding in urban areas is caused by overflowing of drain-water during heavy rains.
Tornado

Tornadoes are vertical funnels of rapidly spinning air. They are formed due to extreme low air pressure, strong convective uplift of air aided by jet streams in upper troposphere. Tip of the tornado always reaches the surface of the Earth, hence it attains its peculiar funnel shape.
Tornado

Tornadoes are accompanied by cumulo-nimbus clouds, strong winds, rain, and sometimes hail. They move at speeds of about 16 to 32 kilometers per hour, and their winds speed can reach up to 402 kilometers per hour.
Lightning

Lightning is a type of extreme weather seen during thunderstorms. Each lightning bolt can contain up to one billion volts of electricity. Lightning is caused in cumulo-nimbus clouds due to discharge of static electricity, during a thunderstorm.
Do you know
The air in the path of the lightning is heated to 54,000°F (30,000°C) within a few thousandths of a second. This makes the air expand explosively, causing the thunder we hear.
Hail

Hailstorms is a form of precipitation, consisting of lumps of ice of different shapes. These are produced from cumulo-nimbus clouds during a thunderstorm. Raindrops are carried upward by the thunderstorm in extremely cold areas of the atmosphere where hails are formed.

2.2 Climatic Changes

Climate change is a change in average climatic conditions of an area. An area can become colder or warmer, wetter, or drier over time. Our Earth is experiencing climatic changes for the last thousands of years. The climate of the Earth was not the same as we are experiencing it today; rather it has undergone various climatic changes in the past.
i. Causes of climate change

There are a number of reasons of climate changes, and the following paragraphs discuss this: Reasons that cause climate changes include the movement of tectonic plates, changes in the Earth's orbit, human activities, and atmospheric changes.
a. Plate Tectonics

The movement of continents over millions of years caused by tectonic plates movement may affect climate changes. The changing position of the continents changes wind flow and ocean currents around the globe. These changes affect the temperature and precipitation patterns of the continents and oceans. Thus, the climate of any particular continent is not the same as it was millions of years ago.
a. Plate Tectonics
Figure: Changing position of the continents — Permian (250 million years ago), Triassic (200 million years ago), Jurassic (145 million years ago), Cretaceous (65 million years ago), Present day.
b. Orbital Changes

i. Changes in the shape of Earth's orbit: Earth's orbit changes from elliptical to circular shape and that affects Earth's distance from the Sun. Earth's distance from the Sun causes climate changes on the Earth. Climatic changes due to changes in the shape of Earth's orbit take place in 100000 years. • ii. Changes in the Earth's tilt:
b. Orbital Changes

Increase or decrease in tilt of Earth's axis results in changes in temperature patterns on Earth's surface, as well as its spinning speed. • iii. The wobble of the Earth on its axis: The wobble of Earth on its axis changes the direction of Earth's tilt and that can change occurrence of seasons. These changes occur in cycles of 26000 years.
c. Human Activities

Amount of carbon dioxide is increasing due to pollution from domestic, agriculture, transport and industrial releases into the atmosphere. Deforestation and burning of trees also release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
c. Human Activities

An increase in carbon dioxide concentrations in atmosphere is leading to global warming. Carbon dioxide molecules retain heat resulting in increase in temperature of atmosphere. Global warming refers to an increase in temperatures around Earth. This increase in temperature causes climate changes in the world.
d. Volcanic Activity

Large volcanic eruptions can influence climates around the world. Sulfur and ash from volcanic eruptions can decrease temperatures by reflecting sunlight back into space. These changes last from a few weeks to several years and depend on the strength and duration of that eruption.
ii. Main threats of Climatic changes

The main threats of climate change include rising sea levels, ecosystem collapse and frequent weather changes and severe weather. Climatic changes affect the whole pattern of weather. It may bring heavy rains or long periods of no rains. Climatic changes also affect crops and vegetation of an area. An area with forests may change into deserts and deserts may change to grasslands or forests.
ii. Main threats of Climatic changes

a. Rise in temperature due to global warming increase the temperature of the polar regions and the oceans. It also cause melting ice cover at the poles and rise in sea level. • b. The warming of the atmosphere affects weather patterns, causing more frequent and severe storms and droughts across the globe.
ii. Main threats of Climatic changes

Higher temperatures are affecting the length of seasons and in some places have already crossed safe levels for survival of ecosystems and humans. • c. The impact of global warming will become more severe if we don't act to stop greenhouse gas emissions.
Effects of climatic changes on life in general

Climatic changes can affect growing patterns of crops, plants and foods. • This change leads to a change in life style of people. • This can lead to migration, a change in economic activities and settlements in new areas may emerge consequently.
2.3 Global Warming

A gradual increase in average global temperature is called global warming. Global temperatures has increased approximately 1°C over the last 100 years. Over the last three decades, human activities have increased the volume of greenhouse gases in air and that has increased the impact of greenhouse effect.

Due to the increase in Greenhouse gases in air, climate of the Earth is becoming warmer. This is termed as Global Warming. Data (gathered from surface weather stations, ships, buoys, balloons, satellites, ice cores, and other palaeoclimatological sources) shows that, over the past 200 years, atmospheric CO₂ concentrations have increased about 35 percent.

Gases of the atmosphere that trap heat are termed as Greenhouse gases. Greenhouse effect refers to the role of carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour in maintaining the atmospheric temperature in a range. As these gases don't let the air temperature drop or rise above a certain level, without Greenhouse effect, our planet would have been 30°C colder than it is today.

Land Pollution
The deposition of solid or liquid waste materials on land or underground that can contaminate the soil and groundwater is called land pollution.
Land Pollution

The waste materials that cause land pollution are broadly classified as municipal solid waste, construction or debris, garbage and trash from our homes. Effects

Soil formation underlying a waste-disposal site reduce the permeability of the soil. The greater the permeability, the greater the risks from land pollution. Soil consists of a mixture of unconsolidated mineral and rock fragments (gravel, sand, silt, and clay) formed from natural weathering processes.
Effects

Gravel and sand formations are porous and permeable—allowing the free flow of water through the pores or spaces between the particles. Silt is much less permeable than sand or gravel, because of its small particle and pore sizes, whereas clay is virtually impermeable to the flow of water because of its platelike shape and molecular forces.

Importance of Ozone Layer

Ozone layer is present in the upper region of our atmosphere, between roughly 15 and 35 km above Earths surface and it contains relatively high concentrations of ozone molecules (O₃). Its presence is essential because it protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation coming from the Sun. Ultraviolet radiations can cause the risk of skin cancer, headaches, eye diseases and other health problems.
Importance of Ozone Layer

It can also damage plant life and aquatic ecosystems. In short, human existence would be difficult without the Ozone layer. Harmful compounds such as Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from air conditioners and refrigerators and oxides of nitrogen and sulphur cause depletion of Ozone layer. This process is known as Ozone depletion. Severe depletion leads to a hole in the Ozone layer that is called ozone hole.
Interesting Fact
Ozone Hole was first ever discovered in 1985 over Antarctica.

Innovation in technology made a considerable change in modes of transport, trade, migration and industrialization. The modern technology has made it easy for people to move from one place to another.
Transportation

Transportation means the movement of goods and persons from one place to another by different modes. Modes of transport can be classified into three groups as land, water and air. 5.1 Modes of Transportation

Modes of transportation means a combination of networks, infrastructures, vehicles and their working. The different modes of transportation are road, railways, air and water. Road Transport

Road transport is the most common and cheap mode of transport. It exists in all parts of the world. This involves the use of vehicles (cars, buses and trucks). Road transport when compared with other modes of transportation, is more flexible. It has high capacity for carrying goods over shorted distances.
Railway Transport

Railway transport is another popular mode of transport in both developed and developing nations in the world. It is used for the movement of both passengers and goods. In many countries they were built specially to access isolated regions and promote political unity. It is one of the oldest mode of transportation that is suitable for transferring bulky goods over long distances.

Air transport is the latest means of transportation that started after the Second World War (WWII). Air transport includes all those man made vehicles and conveyances used to travel and transportation of goods through the air. Some of the examples of air transport are airplanes, helicopters and jet fighter.
Air Transport
It is a very expensive mode of transportation, therefore people prefer road transport over air transport for domestic purposes.

5.2. Role of Transport for the Development of a Settlement

A developed transport system is one of the major reasons for the growth of any settlement. It links producers to markets, workers to jobs, students to schools and the sick to the hospitals. 5.2. Role of Transport for the Development of a Settlement

Efficient and affordable transport system is vital for the development of a settlement. This is a major reason that small towns have been transformed into mega cities due to advanced transport system.
Development of Transport System in Urban and Rural Areas
Urban and rural community is extremely different in term of facilities. There is a vast difference in transportation system between urban and rural areas especially in developing countries.
Transportation in Urban Areas

There is a vast difference in urban and rural transport system. The urban transport system is more developed and organized. Cities have mostly planned and paved roads suitable for heavy traffic. People living in cities have easy access to transport network as they have a lot of options like buses, subways and trains. Although public transport is very crowded it is convenient and fast.
Transportation in Urban Areas

In urban areas local governments continuously work on the repairment, expansion and construction of new roads to meet the needs of high population. For example, overhead bridges and underpasses for pedestrians are fairly common in urban areas.
Transportation in Rural areas

In rural areas, transportation system is not developed and unable to meet the needs of rural population. Poor transportation system directly effects both social and economic situations of these areas. It takes a lot of time to travel from one place to another in rural areas and people have to wait for hours.
Transportation in Rural areas

A major problem with developing and maintaining roads in rural areas is their geographical location, difficult access and limited funds. Government of Pakistan is focusing to improve basic access and promote mobility of rural population through government's poverty reduction program. This target will be achieved by introducing a modern transport system as there are not many developed roads in these regions.

Unit 6: Social and Economic Development

In geography, development refers to the economic and social growth of a country. Development also includes standard of living and quality of life. Standard of living is very high in some countries and on the other hand quality of life is extremely low in other countries. Stage of development is different in all countries. Geographical location is one of the most important reasons of this disparity in the world.

6.1 Measuring Development

Development can be measured by comparing one country with another on the basis of multiple indicators such as social, economic and human. Such indicators of development can be divided into two broad categories.
6.1 Measuring Development
1. Economic Development Indicators • 2. Human Development Indicators
1. Economic Development Indicators
Economic development of a country can be assessed by using economic indicators. Some economic indicators are:
i. Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

GDP is the most important economic indicator to determine the level of development of a country. GDP represents the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced usually in one year, within a country.
i. Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
GDP reflects economic growth and a good standard of living. Thus, the GDP is directly proportional to level of development.
Learning Activity

ii. Gross National Product (GNP)

GNP is referred to the total value of all finished goods and services produced by a country's citizens in a given financial year. It also includes the income received from other countries and excludes any income earned by foreign residents or domestic investments and employment.
Do you know
The World Bank has replaced GNP with Gross National Income (GNI).
iii. Wealth Inequality

Wealth inequality is also known as wealth gap. It is the unequal distribution of wealth or a gap between the rich and the poor in a country. Due to wealth inequality, a few own major portions of the total wealth of the nation. This leaves the remaining population as prey of poverty. On the contrary, where there is less wealth inequality, poverty ratio will be less.
iii. Wealth Inequality
Inequality of wealth exists in developed countries but is high in developing countries.

iv. Inflation

Inflation is the constant increase in aggregate prices of services and goods. It leads to devaluation of the currency of that country, which eventually lowers the values of the savings of the country's residents. It also decreases the purchasing power of the people of that country. High inflation is bad for economic development, while lower inflation rate is considered good for economic development.
v. Unemployment

Unemployment is the state of economy where the individuals are unable to get jobs even though they are eligible for employment. It is due to unavailability of work. High rate of unemployment indicates the low level of development.

6.3 Economic Activities

Economic activities determine the level of development of a country. Economic activity refers to the human activities or efforts for the purpose of livelihood and income generation. Geographers categorize human economic activities into five groups:
1. Primary Economic Activities:
These activities are directly related to the nature or extraction of resources of the Earth. Agriculture, livestock farming, forestry, fishing, mining are some of the important primary activities.
2. Secondary Economic Activities:

These activities use raw materials produced by primary activities and change their form into more valuable finished goods. Secondary economic activities include industry, manufacturing and construction.
3. Tertiary Economic Activities:

These activities provide a wide range of services to primary and secondary activities. Important tertiary activities include clerical and financial services, trade (retail and wholesale), transport and communication.
4. Quaternary Economic Activities:

These activities are related to special type of services and often closely linked with tertiary activities. Examples of quaternary activities include Educational Services, Health Services, Recreational Services and Information Technology.
5. Quinary Economic Activities:

These activities are relatively new and associated with high intellectuals. Scientists, researchers, policy makers, and top executives (highest level decision-makers) are some of the important professionals engaged in quinary activities.

6.4 Role of Inflation and Unemployment in the Development

Cost of living increases when the inflation rate is high, which also leads to low level of development. Inflation can sometimes cause unemployment when the uncertainty of inflation leads to low investment and low economic growth in the long term. Customer purchases few goods during high unemployment, which sometimes reduces inflation.

High unemployment rate leads to negative impact on development because unemployed people waste resources without contributing to the economy. Unemployment can cause illness, conflicts and social unrest in the country. In developed countries unemployed people put extra burden on the economy by taking benefits of joblessness. Unemployment is low in many developing countries, because jobless benefits are uncommon.

Arrival of the British in India

The British started arriving in India in the 16th century AD when Queen Elizabeth-I sent ships to the Subcontinent. Later, in the first half of seventeenth century the British East India Company opened its offices in India. Mughal rulers gave significant trade concessions to the British. Along with trade, the British East India Company was involved in the politics of India.
Arrival of the British in India

In next few decades, the British became so strong that they started challenging the local rulers. At the same time, some areas of India were influenced by the French thus making the Subcontinent another battle ground for the two rivals.
East India Company
It was a British trade company formed under a charter by Queen Elizabeth-I in 1600 AD. It comprised of British merchants and aristocrats.
Battle of Plassey (1757) and the British Rise to Power in Bengal

Battle of Plassey 1757 is an important milestone in the history of the Subcontinent. In this battle, East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-Ud-Daulah thus strengthened their position in Bengal.
Battle of Plassey (1757) and the British Rise to Power in Bengal

The British wanted to protect their business in India but Siraj-ud-Daulah was inclined towards the French. In this way he was a big hurdle for the British interests. This made the British think to get rid of him. The Commander in Chief of the British Army in India, Robert Clive, was aware of the superior military strength of the Nawab.
Battle of Plassey (1757) and the British Rise to Power in Bengal
For this reason, they bribed Nawab's General Mir Jaffar whose treachery helped the British to win the war against Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah.

The war did not last long. During the war, Nawab's artillery was dampened because of heavy rainfall. On the other hand, the British forces were able to keep their ammunition safe which changed the course of war. This victory of the British was significant in many ways. They were not only able to take a lead against the French but were also encouraged to capture other parts of India.
Battle of Plassey (1757) and the British Rise to Power in Bengal
The historians believe that victory in the battle of Plassey paved the way of colonization for the British in the Subcontinent.
Battle of Buxar

During the battle of Plassey, military commander of the Siraj-Ud-Daulah's forces was Mir Jaffar who helped the British East India Company. After the defeat, Siraj-Ud-Daulah was dethroned as the Nawab of Bengal and Mir Jaffar was made the Nawab of Bengal. He was only a puppet in the hands of the British, but his rule could not last long. Soon, Mir Jaffar's son-in-law Mir Qasim was throned as the new Nawab.
Causes of the Battle

The expectations of the British could not be completely fulfilled by Mir Qasim who started trying to be independent of the British influence. Some of the steps of Mir Qasim were not liked by the British which included shifting of his capital from Calcutta to Munger Fort, not giving extra privileges to the British traders.
Causes of the Battle

Mir Qasim was not pleased with the increasing demands of the British, hence, he formed an alliance with Nawab of Oudh and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. In this background, the British decided to remove Mir Qasim from the throne and this started a battle between Mir Qasim and the East India Company. This battle is known as battle of Buxar.
Causes of the Battle

The Battle

Confrontations started in 1763 with a series of victories by the British. Mir Qasim fled to Oudh where he gathered with the Nawab of Oudh Shuja-Ud-Daula and the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. Mir Qasim's forces faced the English army in 1764. The British forces were led by Major Hector Munro.
The Battle

It was a battle between 40,000 men from Mir Qasim's combined forces and 10,000 British force and the joint armies were defeated by the British. The main reason of this defeat was lack of coordination among the combined forces. As a result of this battle, Mir Qasim fled from the battleground while the other two: Nawab of Oudh and Shah Alam II surrendered. The battle ended with the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765.
The Battle
According to the Treaty of Allahabad Nawab Shuja was forced to surrender Allahabad and Kara to Shah Alam II, and he was obliged to pay the East India Company a war compensation of 5 million rupees.

War of Independence 1857 is one of the most important landmarks of the Subcontinent history. This was the last effort of the people of the Subcontinent to get rid of British dominance. There were many causes behind this war that include, political, social, religious and economic reasons. Some of the causes are mentioned here:
War of Independence

Humiliation of Mughal rulers by the ruling British regime. • Rude behavior of the British towards the local Indians. The British never mixed with the locals and considered themselves superior to others. • Christian missionaries were sent to spread their religion. Local Indians considered them a threat for their religions. • Heavy taxes were imposed on the landlords.
War of Independence

Their lands were also confiscated in case they were not able to provide documentary evidence of their ancestral lands. • Many states were annexed by the British on the grounds of poor governance. This made the rulers of those states enemy of the British. • Doctrine of lapse and annexation policy of the British.
Immediate Cause

The Indian soldiers in the British forces were issued cartridges greased with fat of pigs and cows. In order to use those cartridges, the soldiers had to bite their end. The Muslim and the Hindu soldiers in Meerut refused to use those cartridges. It was considered a rebellion and those soldiers were arrested and jailed. Unsuccessful War of Independence had very bad consequences for the people of the Subcontinent. The Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured, his two sons and a grandson were killed, and he was sent to Rangoon (Myanmar) where he died in the year 1862 AD.

Hundreds and thousands of people were brutally murdered. The Muslims were subjected to greater oppression as in the eyes of the British, they were the main cause of the War of Independence. Unsuccessful War of Independence 1857 proved to be disastrous for the people of the Subcontinent. Despite all kinds of sacrifices, the war could not be successful. At the same time, it caused strengthening of British rule in the region. Following the failed War of Independence, the rule of East India Company came to an end.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858
On November 1, 1858, it was announced that the Queen had assumed the government of India. Queen Victoria's Proclamation declared that India would be governed through a Secretary of State.
Salient Features of Proclamation
Salient features of the Queen Victoria Proclamation are:
Salient Features of Proclamation

(i) A Viceroy was appointed to run the government affairs in India. • (ii) State princes were assured that treaties made by East India Company would be honoured. • (iii) Religious freedom was restored as the servants of the British government in India were ordered not to interfere in the religious affairs of the local people. • (iv) Equal treatment was promised to Indians.
Salient Features of Proclamation
• (v) Local people were assured that due regard would be given to their customs while framing and administering any law.
Salient Features of Proclamation
The proclamation of 1858 AD was indeed a landmark in the History of India. This declaration of policy remained the basis of Indian administration till the 20th century.
British Administration in India

After the failed War of Independence 1857, the British government abolished Mughal Dynasty. The last Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Burma (Myanmar). British Governor General took the control of India who was the representative of the British parliament. Though many princely states were kept intact, their princes were pressurized to cooperate with the British.
British Administration in India
Viceroy Canning adopted a policy of punishing resistance and rewarding obedience. Thus, many faithful princes were rewarded by him. In this way, the British kept effective control over India.
British Administration in India

After 1858, Great Britain ruled about 60% of India directly and the other 40% indirectly through native princes. The British developed agriculture and industries. At the same time, the British developed infrastructure with huge railway network. The judicial, police, and taxation systems were organized efficiently. Education, health services and local government were also improved significantly.
British Administration in India

A member from British parliament was given the title of Secretary of State for India who was empowered to run affairs of the country. For proper implementation of the policies a 15-member council was also constituted under the chairmanship of Secretary of State. The title of the Governor General was changed to Viceroy, who was given the authority to appoint the governors.

The British were aware of the fact that in the face of absolute monarchy over many centuries, the people of the Subcontinent could not have their say in the affairs of the government. British Education Policy

Before the British, India had its own educational system. Education in the Subcontinent had always been of a classical and spiritual rather of a practical nature. Languages of instruction were Arabic, Persian and Sanskrit, which were sacred classical languages of the Muslims and the Hindus. However, under the British more emphasis was put on modern education.
British Education Policy

Under the British rule, educational policies in India were shaped by the colonial interests. However, during the first hundred years of the East India Company, no attention was given to education. The Charter Act of 1813 was turning point in the history of education in the Subcontinent. With this Act education became one of the duties of the Company.
British Education Policy

Section 43 of this Act defined the objectives of the educational policy which included 'the revival and improvement of literature', 'the encouragement of learned natives of India' and 'the introduction and promotion of a knowledge of sciences among the inhabitants of the British territories in India'.
British Education Policy

In 1823, General Committee of Public Instruction was formed which was to guide the East India Company. There was a clear difference of opinion among the members in deciding whether eastern education is to be preferred or the western one. This controversy continued till 1836 when Lord Macaulay presented his famous minute.
Lord Macaulay's Minute (1836-37)

On February 2, 1836 Macaulay presented his famous minute. He declared more funding for English and scientific education. He declared English as the key to success and declared Arabic, Persian and Sanskrit as inferior languages. Following words present true depiction of British education policy in India:
Lord Macaulay's Minute (1836-37)
"We must at present do our best to form a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals and in intellect".
Lord Macaulay's Minute (1836-37)

Macaulay further expressed his preference for higher education for the upper class at the cost of ignoring elementary classes. He believed that the education from the upper class could be transmitted to lower class, but this could never happen. The result of Macaulay's minute was systematic wiping out of traditional Indian education system and sciences.
Note for Teachers
The students may be asked to learn more about Lord Macaulay's minute and its significance for the education system of Pakistan.
Wood's Despatch (1854)

In order to review the education policies followed by East India Company, a special parliamentary committee was appointed to suggest educational policy for India. After a thorough evaluation, the Committee presented a policy document on education. As Charles Wood was the President of the Board of Control for India, this document was called "Wood's Despatch".
Wood's Despatch (1854)

The objective of this Despatch was raising the moral character and supply of servants, in addition to producing a higher degree of intellectual fitness. The function of education was to spread European arts, philosophy, science and literature through English and other languages of India. Wood stressed on the importance of useful education for the public.
Wood's Despatch (1854)

Education under the East India Company ended with the Wood's Despatch of 1854 as the Company was abolished in 1858 and the Government of India came directly under the British government. In 1882, Hunter Commission was formed to evaluate the achievements of Wood Despatch of 1854. This commission underlined the state's role in the improvement of elementary and secondary education.
Wood's Despatch (1854)
It also highlighted the transfer of control to district boards and recommended two divisions of secondary education up to university and vocational for commercial career.
Colonial Economic Policy in India
Since the early 19th century, Indian economy served the profits for the British rulers. Salient features of the Colonial Economic Policy in India were:
Colonial Economic Policy in India

i) The Subcontinent was used both as a supplier of raw materials as well as market of goods produced in Britain. • ii) Revenue was collected from the local people, but it was then spent in buying goods that were then transported to Britain. • iii) Many irrigation schemes were initiated to bring more land under cultivation.
Colonial Economic Policy in India

• iv) Heavy taxes were levied on people, especially on farmers to meet the high expenditure on salary of the British army officers and officials. • v) Ownership of properties law was introduced, and free trade was encouraged.
Colonial Economic Policy in India

Many of the policies made in the name of uplifting of the local people resulted in further poverty. Economic policies of the British did not allow the rise of modern Industries as had happened in other European countries.
Note for Teachers
The students may be encouraged to find more information about colonial economic policies in India. They may share the reasons of continued poverty in the country.
Social Transformation

Initially East India Company kept the policy of non-interference in the social life of the people of the Subcontinent. However, in later years and specially after 1857, many changes occurred in the lives of the people. Contact of the local people with the West made educated people feel that social transformation was necessary for development of the country.
Social Transformation
Following are few of the social reforms introduced by the British:
Social Transformation

i) Sati (the practice of burning a Hindu widow with her dead husband) was made illegal and punishable by law. • ii) Slavery was made illegal. • iii) The Widow Remarriage Act was passed. • iv) Prevailing caste system was discouraged, and people were provided equal opportunities. • v) Female education was promoted. • vi) Underage marriages were banned, and minimum age was fixed for marriage.
Development of Communication Network

One of the distinct features of the British rule in India was incredible development of communication network. As the Industrial Revolution gained momentum, the manufacturing increased manifold in England. This required both the raw material as well as market for the manufactured goods.
Development of Communication Network
The British found both these in the Subcontinent and instead of exporting manufactured products, India was forced to export raw materials like raw cotton and silk to Britain.
Development of Communication Network
Figure: Khojak Tunnel in Balochistan was built in 1891.
Development of Communication Network

The demands of an industrialised England required better communication facilities in the Subcontinent. The British realised that a cheaper and faster transport system was necessary for increasing trade volume. They introduced steamships on the rivers and improved existing roads beside constructing new roads. Grand Trunk Road from Calcutta to Delhi was improved in the 1850s.
Development of Communication Network

Keeping in view the military and business interests, a huge railway system was built. By 1859, the passenger train was started in the Subcontinent. Besides serving the business and military interests of the British, the railway also provided employment and business to the locals.

Muslims after the Decline of the Mughal Empire

After the death of Aurangzeb Alamgir in 1707 AD, the Mughal Empire was facing decline in both power and authority. There were numerous causes behind the lost glory of the Mughals such as economic bankruptcy, loss of nobility, weak rulers, rebellions and invasions by the foreign rulers. Moreover, the Mughal army lost its capacity to fight because of obsolete weapons and constant infighting.
Muslims after the Decline of the Mughal Empire
The Indians were becoming increasingly concerned about preserving their faiths, culture, traditions, and society.
Muslim Scholars in Subcontinent
The efforts for the Muslim awakening and impact of influential Muslim scholars started to appear at the horizon of Subcontinent in the 17th century during the reign of Mughal emperor Akbar.
Muslim Scholars in Subcontinent

Sheikh Ahmad Sarhindi-Mujaddid Alf Sani, Shah Wali Ullah, Syed Ahmad Shaheed Bareilvi and Haji Shariat Ullah were recognized for their prolific services for the regeneration of Islamic society in the history of the Muslims of Subcontinent.
Introduction

Sheikh Ahmad Sarhindi al-Farooqi an-Naqshbandi was born on 26 June 1564. His father Sheikh Abdul Ahad was a prominent Muslim Sufi scholar of his time. Sheikh Ahmed obtained his basic education in Quran, Hadith, Tafseer, Philosophy and theology from Sarhind. During this time, Islamic teachings were in decline because Muslim scholars and Ulama neglected the necessity of the actual teachings of Quran and Sunnah.
Introduction
He wrote many books and described the vitality of Quran and Prophethood for the Muslims and the humanity.
Main Contributions
Sheikh Ahmed Sarhindi quickly rose to the pinnacle of experience and vision and made extraordinary contributions to revival of Islam. Some of his important services are outlined as follows;
i. Fight Against Deen-e-Ilahi

Mughal Emperor Akbar presented Deen-e-Ilahi that was combination of the teachings of Hindu and Muslim beliefs and doctrines of some local religions. Sheikh Ahmed Sarhindi described it as an attack on Islam and vowed to eradicate the ambiguous religious teachings from daily lives of Muslims.
i. Fight Against Deen-e-Ilahi
His efforts became successful when Emperor Jahangir canceled all those orders of his father Akbar which were against the teachings of Islam and hence, the infamous Deen-e-Ilahi came to an end.
Facts to Know
Islamic followers have referred to Sheikh Ahmad Sarhindi as a Mujaddid, or "reviver," for his work in reviving Islam and opposing the newly formed religion of Deen-e-Ilahi.

Maktubat-e-Imam Rabbani

Maktub in Urdu means letter. Sheikh Ahmed wrote letters to the noble personnel of the royal court. These letters were focused on persuading the princes and nobles to understand teachings of Islam and to show the right path to the people and kings.
Importance

Sheikh Ahmed was a role model for the Muslims. He laid stress on practicing the true and pure Islamic principles in all walks of life. • His biggest milestone achievement was his resistance against Deen-e-Ilahi which highlighted the need for revival of true Islamic practices.
Importance
Sheikh Ahmad Sarhindi spent his life in working towards making people adhere with the actual and factually laid down path of Islam. He continued his preaching of Islam till the end of his life.
Importance
Figure: Tomb of Mujaddid Alf Sani.
Introduction

Shah Wali Ullah was born on 21 February 1703. His real name was Qutub-ud-din but later on he was known as Shah Wali Ullah due to his piety. His father, Shah Abdul Rahim, a well-known religious scholar, established Madrasah Rahimiya in Delhi. Shah Wali Ullah also taught in Madrasah Rahimiya and became a role model for his students.
Introduction
In 1724, during his visit to Hejaz (Saudi Arabia), Shah Wali Ullah received further education from Sheikh Abu Tahir bin Ibrahim.
Introduction

After the death of Aurangzeb Alamgir, Mughal Empire was declining. The Muslims were disunited and their religion was vulnerable to attacks. According to Shah Wali Ullah, these issues were partly the result of incomplete knowledge of Quran and Hadith. He also realized that the Muslim community needed strong leadership particularly in Delhi.
Introduction
He wanted Muslims to follow Islamic morals and spiritual teachings in their social, economic and political lives.
i. Translation of the Holy Quran

Shah Wali Ullah desired that Muslims should understand the teachings of Islam. Hence he translated Holy Quran in Persian language because there were very less people who could speak Arabic. Later on, his two sons Shah Abdul Qadir and Shah Rafi translated the Holy Quran in Urdu langauge.
ii. Scholarly Works

Shah Wali Ullah promoted his message through his writings and teachings. He wrote fifty-one books in Persian and Arabic. Among his writings, Hujjat Allah al- Baligha and Izalat al-Khafa'an Khilafat al-Khulfa were important contributions.
Facts to Know

Hujjat Allah al- Baligha is described as the writing of the 'theological sociology' which is comprised of synthetic work of philosophy, history, law, theology, psychoanalysis of human nature. In this book, Shah Wali Ullah interpreted Sharia as the body of injunction that is in alliance with natural human tendency to behave.
iii. Opposition to Marathas and Restoration of Mughal Empire

One of the greatest contributions of Shah Wali Ullah was his organization of opposition against the growing power of Marathas. They were threatening to suppress the Mughal Empire. Shah Wali Ullah realized that Muslim unity was required and hence wrote to various noble Muslims to join hands to overthrow Marathas in order to restore the declining Mughal Empire.
iii. Opposition to Marathas and Restoration of Mughal Empire
Ahmed Shah Abdali along with local Muslim leaders defeated Marathas at Panipat in 1761 and restored the Mughal Empire.
iv. Bridging the Differences Among Muslims

Shah Wali Ullah bridged the gap between various Muslim sects through his writings and speeches. He believed that the pathway to the Muslim revival would pass through the clarity of concepts about the fundamentals of Islam and reconciliation among different sects. Shah Wali Ullah wrote Izalat al-Khafa'an Khilafat al-Khulfa meaning "Removal of Ambiguity about the Caliphate of the [Early] Caliphs".
iv. Bridging the Differences Among Muslims
This book was highly acclaimed as the main source of political thought of Shah Wali Ullah.
iv. Bridging the Differences Among Muslims

Shah Wali Ullah's ideas motivated the Muslims in times of despair. The influence of his teachings lasted for long even after his death. His followers kept promoting his ideas and teachings including his sons Shah Abdul Aziz, Shah Abdul Qadir and Shah Rafiuddin. Many supporters of the Pakistan movement believed that they were building on the idea of "two nations" posited in Shah Wali Ullah's works.

Introduction

Syed Ahmed was born in 1786, in Rai Bareli which is a small town near Lucknow. He received his education of Quran and Hadith from the sons of Shah Wali Ullah in Madrasah Rahimiya. In 1810, he also learned to use the European weaponry. He was given the command of the group of soldiers due to his capabilities. Owing to his piety he was also tasked with leading the troop's prayers.
Introduction

Syed Ahmed was committed to the idea of Jihad and desired that Muslims must liberate themselves from non- Muslim rule through armed struggle against the British domination and Sikh regime in North-West Frontier.
Vision of Jihad to liberate Muslims

British Crown allowed the domination of Sikhs in Punjab in terms of power and authority. Syed Ahmed founded his jihad movement which called for armed struggle aiming at overthrowing the non-Muslim oppressive rule. Upon his return from Hijaz (Present day Saudi Arabia) in 1823, Syed Ahmed travelled all over Punjab, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, (continued on the next page)

(continued) Rajasthan and Sindh to recruit his forces and established his headquarters in Peshawar. Ranjit Singh denied Syed Ahmad's demands for granting the Muslims' rights of religious freedom.
Vision of Jihad to liberate Muslims

Syed Ahmad started Jihad firstly against the Sikh regime at Akora and later captured Peshawar successfully. These military expeditions lasted for two months and caused defeat to the Sikhs which established Syed Ahmad as an efficient military leader.
Vision of Jihad to liberate Muslims

However, a few defections among the troops caused split in his forces. Syed Ahmed fought a fierce battle at Balakot in 1831. Around six hundred soldiers martyred in this battle along with Syed Ahmed Shaheed Barelvi.
Vision of Jihad to liberate Muslims
