Importance

i. He started the Jihad movement aiming to liberate the Muslims from the non-Muslims and the foreign domination. His desire to sacrifice for the cause of Islam was an inspiration for others. • ii. He invoked the desire in the hearts of the Muslims to demand religious and spiritual freedom. • iii. Many historians term Jihad movement as the leading force of motivation for the Pakistan Movement in India. • iv.
Importance
He persuaded Muslims to defend their culture, religion and their identity.
Introduction

Haji Shariat-ullah was born in the district of Faridabad, East Bengal, in 1781. He stayed in Saudi Arabia for nineteen years and performed pilgrimage in 1799. He was greatly influenced by the beliefs of Sheikh Muhammad Abdul Wahab. After his return to the East Bengal, he started his own reform movement aiming to purify Islam from the influence of Hindu practices and to empower the Muslim community in East Bengal.
Introduction
After his death in 1840, his legacy was carried forward by his sons.
Note for Teachers (Group Activity)
Jihad Movement by Syed Ahmed Barelvi was a uniting force for Muslims. • Divide the class into two groups and ask them to write down five points regarding the need and the importance of this movement.
Faraizi Movement

Haji Shariat-Ullah wanted Muslims to return to their true roots by proper observation of Islamic duties called faraiz. His movement was known as Faraizi Movement. He realized that Muslims of Bengal were in constant state of oppression by both British and Hindus. Muslims were mistreated by the British rulers and oppressed by the Hindu Zamindars.
Faraizi Movement

His teachings led to the religious and spiritual revival which brought them back to the folds of Islamic teachings. He also provided a platform to the Bengali peasants to get united against the discriminatory economic policies of the British and Hindus against the Muslims.
Faraizi Movement
Figure: Map of divided Bengal which became the originating point for the Faraizi Movement.
Continuation of the Legacy

After his death in 1840, his work was carried forward by his son Mohsin-ud-din. He worked tirelessly to enhance the conditions of the Muslims in East Bengal through the introduction of various important economic measures.
Hindu Revivalist Movements

During the 17th and the 19th Century, certain Hindu reformist as well as revivalist movements began in the Subcontinent which aimed at the revival of the Hinduism in societal, spiritual and religious aspects.
Hindu Revivalist Movements

From the 18th century onwards, the British rule impacted the social and religious fabric of the Subcontinent through its agenda of colonization. This caused the inculcation of the western cultures and ethos in the local cultures causing the state of worry for the Hindu religious scholars. They struggled to counter the growing influence of westernization on Hindu identity and culture through the revival movements.
1. Brahmo Samajh

It was monotheistic reformist movement of Hindu religion that was prominent during the Bengal Renaissance in 19th Century. It was founded in Calcutta by Ram Mohun Roy. He was also known as the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance'.
Note for Teachers (Group Activity)

Divide the class in groups and assign each Muslim Scholar to one group accordingly. Instruct them to discuss the salient contributions of each scholar towards the revival of Islam and highlight the lessons that can be drawn for the Muslims of today.
Importance

i. This movement fought against the notion of cast oppression that was prevalent in India at that time. • ii. Align with that, it also resisted the ideology of polytheism. This movement fought against the idol worship and the suppression of women. It also created awareness about superstitions.
2. Arya Samajh

Arya Samajh was a Hindu revivalist based on a monotheistic notion that emphasized on the values and practices originated from the absolute authority of Vedas (large body of religious text in Sanskrit). It was founded in 10th April in 1875 by Mullah Shankar who is also known as Swami Dayananda Saraswati.
2. Arya Samajh

He devised the slogan "Go Back to Vedas". The main aim of the movement was to re-establish the old Hindu scriptures as the revealed truths and to improve the physical and spiritual well-being of all the mankind.
2. Arya Samajh
Figure: Swami Dayananda Saraswati.
Importance

This movement fought against caste determination and idolatry. The two controversial movements; Cow Protection Movement and the Conversion Movement were initiated in 1882, just before his death. These principles are still being followed in Arya Samajh.
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (1817-1898)

After the war, the British regained control of India and established their rule. The British, however, became more hostile towards muslims. Muslims lost their steady jobs in the police force, as lawyers, in the army and in the government. Muslims believed the British were aiming to subvert their religion and culture. Many muslims refused to cooperate with the British which strained their relations.
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (1817-1898)
In such circumstances, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan began a lifelong campaign to improve Muslim-British relations and Muslim status in British India.
Note for Teachers (Group Activity)

Engage the students in a critical debate related to the parallel occurrences of Muslim and Hindu religious revivalism and overall impacts on the Indian society. • Divide the class in groups and hold a debate on the topic "Was India more difficult to govern after 1857-58?"
The Aligarh Movement

Aligarh Movement was started in 1875 with the establishment of the Muhammadan Anglo Oriental School at Aligarh in Uttar Pradesh (UP). After two years, the status of the school was upgraded to college in 1877 and the oriental and western education was provided. Many Muslims began studying at Aligarh College, which eventually transformed it into a center of excellence for Muslim learning.
The Aligarh Movement
Figure: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan.
Aims of the Aligarh Movement
Following were the main aims of the Aligarh Movement:
Aims of the Aligarh Movement

Improving the Muslim-British relationships by developing better understanding. • Encouraging Muslims to pursue Western education in order to obtain positions in the civil service and the military. • Educate Muslims about their political rights and face challenges to their social and political standing as compared to Hindus.
Political Contribution
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was strong advocate of British-Muslim harmony. According to Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, following two reasons were vital for the improvement of relations between the two:
Political Contribution

i. Eradicating the misconceived notion of Muslims by the British which was distorted by the belief that Muslims were primarily to be blamed for the events of the War of 1857 and hence deserved to be suppressed. • ii. Muslims considered that Western ideas conflicted with Islamic teachings. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, on the other hand, urged Muslims to benefit from Western science and technology.
Social Contribution

In his pursuance of defending Muslims' position, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan wrote many scholarly writings to build the case of Muslims as loyal to the British government. These include 'The loyal Muhammadans of India 1860', 'Essay on the Causes of Indian Revolt' and 'Tabbyin-ul-Kalam', (similarities between Islam and Christianity).
Educational Contribution

Sir Syed Ahmad Khan aspired to transform Muslims' educational achievement by instilling a desire for high-quality education. There were around 711 Hindus in the administration in 1871, compared to only 92 Muslims. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan wanted Muslims to understand the need of education for progression and to be able to exercise their political and administrative rights.
Educational Contribution
He believed that the Holy Quran emphasizes the importance of obtaining scientific education which contributes to comprehending Allah Almighty's entire magnificence.
Educational Contribution

His contributions include opening of schools in Muradabad and Ghazipur, replicating British education for the Muslims of India, opening of Muhammadan Anglo Oriental College and organization of Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1886.
Facts to Know

Sir Syed also cleared British misunderstanding regarding the use of word "Nazareth" by the Muslims. This was considered as insult by British but Sir Syed cleared that the origin of this word came from 'Nasir', an Arabic word meaning helper. Hence, this term was reflection of positive image of British in the minds of Muslims instead of an insult.
Educational Contribution
Figure: Aligarh Muslim University.
Significance

The important role played by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan during the depressing years of Muslim history in the Subcontinent was the driving force behind the movement of education prosperity for Muslim community. He convinced both British and Muslims to review their rigid approach towards each other and focus on the mutual cooperation.
Significance

He made Muslims realized the vitality of the education and its significance in improving the socio-economic status of Muslims in the community. His tireless efforts resulted as the era of renaissance for Muslims in terms of political awareness and realization pertaining to the value of education. Owing to these contributions, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan is rightly titled as the "Father of the Pakistan Movement".
Do You Know?

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan developed his two-nation idea for a reason. Sir Syed Ahmed recognized that, as a minority, the western democratic system of political representation was not in the best interest of Muslim community.
Do You Know?

Sir Syed's opinion that Congress party was working against the Muslims' interests, led him to create the two-nation theory which states that Muslims and Hindus cannot coexist and that Muslims should be treated as a separate country due to fundamental differences. To hope that both could remain equal is to desire the impossible and the inconceivable.
Contributions of Muslim Educational Institutions

Apart from the Aligarh Movement, notable educational institutions such as Anjuman Himayat-i-Islam, Sindh Madrassa-tul-Islam, Islamia College Peshawar, Darul Uloom Deoband, and Nadva tul Ulama Lucknow also played a role in the resurgence of Muslims across the Subcontinent.
Contributions of Muslim Educational Institutions

i. Darul Uloom Deoband: Darul Uloom Deoband was established in 1867 in Deoband, Saharanpur (Utter Pardesh), India. This organisation worked to safeguard Muslims' religious, social, and educational endowments. Aside from religious education, several skills were also taught such as calligraphy and cloth weaving etc. • ii. Nadva tul Ulama: Nadva tul Ulama was created in Lucknow in 1894.
Contributions of Muslim Educational Institutions

A composite syllabus comprising English, Science, and religious subjects was taught at the primary level. The Muslims of the Subcontinent benefited greatly from the alumni of this institution. Darul Uloom produced such open-minded academics who successfully carried out the task of spreading Islam in the modern world.
Contributions of Muslim Educational Institutions

iii. Sindh Madrassa-tul-Islam: Sindh Madrassa-tul-Islam evolved into a magnificent blend of modern and religious education. Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, studied in Sindh Madrassa-tul-Islam from 1877 to 1892. The historical significance of Sindh Madrassa-tul-Islam extends beyond that of a pivotal educational institution during the Pakistan Movement.
Introduction

Syed Ameer Ali was British/Indian Jurist who hailed from the state of Oudh. He was born on 6 April 1849 at Cuttack in Odisha. His father moved the family to Calcutta. He graduated from Calcutta University in 1867 and gained an MA degree with Honors in History in 1868. The LLB degree followed quickly in 1869. He then began legal practice in Calcutta.
Introduction
Up till then he already became one of the highest Muslim achiever of his generation.
Introduction

In 1882 he became a member of the Imperial Legislative Council. In 1890, he was appointed as a high court judge. Ameer Ali was the first Indian who was nominated as a member of Privy Council to which he remained a member till his death on 3rd August 1928.
1. Literary Contribution

Ameer Ali is famous for his literary work along with his political efforts and achievements. He was the author of two famous works one of which is the History of Saracens published in 1889 that tells the story of the rise and fall of Saracens. The other work is the Spirit of Islam published in 1891. He also wrote articles mainly countering anti-Muslim articles of a Christian.
2. Political Contribution

When Sir Syed Ahmed Khan was strongly against the Muslim participation in politics, Ameer Ali founded a political organization in the year 1878 called National Mohammadan Association at Calcutta. This was later known as Central Mohammadan Association and a lot of its branches began working all over India.
2. Political Contribution
He believed that the status of Muslims as an independent nation in India would not be possible without their own political (continued on the next page)

organization. That was the major aim of the establishment of Central Mohammadan Association. The main objectives were as under;

Political training of the Muslims • Conservation of Muslim interests • Establishment of good feelings among the followers of different faiths in India

What I have learned

• One of the distinct features of the British rule in India was the development of communication network including the huge rail network. • After the unsuccessful War of Independence of 1857, the Muslims faced wrath of the British as they were considered the main cause of the war. • During the time of distress, Sir Syed Ahmed Khan made educational, social and political efforts to improve the lives of the Muslims.

The League of Nations was an international diplomatic group developed after World War I. It was founded in 1920 as a way to solve disputes between countries before they turn to large wars. Political Awakening in India

In the previous chapters, we have read that after failure of War of Independence in 1857, the Indians learnt that they could not get rid of the British through military means and that they would have to live with them. In these circumstances, Indian National Congress was formed in 1885 to protect and enhance the feeling of unity among all Indians without any distinction.
Political Awakening in India
Moreover, it was to fix up those aims and means which were to be adopted by the Indian politicians for the welfare of India.
The Formation of Congress in 1885

During the later half of the 19th century, nationalism and political consciousness grew in the Subcontinent. After the War of Independence in 1857, the locals understood that independence could not be achieved through military means. In these circumstances, the Indian National Congress was formed in 1885. Allan Octavian Hume, a retired civil servant played an instrumental role in formulation of Congress.
The Formation of Congress in 1885

The main objects of the Congress were to protect and enhance the feeling of unity among all Indians without distinction of caste, religion, and province. Moreover, it was to fix up those aims and means which were to be adopted by the Indian politicians for the welfare of India.
The Formation of Congress in 1885

The formation of Congress is a turning point in formalizing opposition to the British rule. While the Indian National Congress claimed to represent all the people without any discrimination, it did not remain unbiased. Under such circumstances, the Muslims of the Subcontinent needed to form their own political platform. This need paved the way for the establishment of the All India Muslim League.
Simla Deputation

A delegation of prominent Muslim leaders from all over India led by Sir Aga Khan met Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla on October 1,1906. After War of Independence, it was for the first time that Muslims presented their demands on constitutional plan. The Viceroy gave a patient hearing to Muslims and promised sympathetic consideration to the demands. Simla Deputation turned as a landmark in history of India.
Simla Deputation
It led to foundation of All India Muslim League and Identity of Indian Muslims as a separate nation.
All India Muslim League
The All India Muslim League was established at Dhaka in 1906. The main reasons for the formation of the Muslim League were:
All India Muslim League

The Indian National Congress could not maintain its neutral attitude and it became the mouthpiece of the Hindus only. By 1906, the Muslim leaders were convinced that having their own political party which will speak for the Muslims on all important occasions is absolutely necessary. • The Urdu-Hindi controversy began with the demand of the Hindus to replace Urdu by Hindi as the official language.
All India Muslim League
The Congress visibly sided with Hindi and supported the (continued on the next page)
All India Muslim League
movement against Urdu. At that moment, the need of formation of a Muslim party was felt severely.
All India Muslim League

At the time of announcement of Minto-Morley Reforms, the Muslims did not have any platform from where they could share their demands. It made them think more seriously about forming a separate party. • The ideology presented by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan regarding the separate identity of the Muslims appealed to many people. It became essential for the Muslims to establish a political party of their own.
All India Muslim League

• The Muslims of the Subcontinent remained backward as compared to the Hindus in education and economic progress. A separate Muslim organization was necessary to safeguard the interests of the Muslims.
All India Muslim League

The establishment of the All India Muslim League was one of the most important milestones in the history and struggle for freedom. After its establishment, the Muslim League rendered great services for the Muslims of the Subcontinent including the right to separate electorate in 1909. Mostly, the line of action of the Muslim League was different than that of the Congress.
All India Muslim League

However, annulment of partition of Bengal and Kanpur Masjid incident caused deep anguish among the Muslims. Muslims League changed its strategy from loyalty to demand of self-rule suitable to Indian conditions.

Change in political objectives of All India Muslim League was an important event. It paved the way for Quaid's inclusion in Muslim League who, simultaneously continued to be a member of the Congress which he had joined in 1913.

Being staunch supporter of Hindu-Muslim unity, Quaid-e-Azam utilized his pivotal position to bring the Congress and the Muslim League closer to work out common solutions to problems faced by Indians. 1915 and 1916. The main outcome of these sessions was Congress League pact of 1916 called Lucknow Pact. The Congress agreed right of separate electorate for the Muslims and one third representation in Imperial Legislative Council.
Lucknow Pact 1916

Lucknow Pact was an important event in the history of the Muslims of South Asia. For the first time Congress recognized the Muslim League as representative of the Muslims of the region. As Congress agreed to separate electorates, it in fact considered the Muslims of Subcontinent as a separate nation. The demand for Self-rule of Congress and League moved the British Government for constitutional reforms in India.

Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms

Through Lucknow Pact 1916, Congress and League accommodated each other's claims by setting aside mutual differences and called for greater self-government. Feeling the pressure, the British introduced Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms in 1918 which provided basis for Government of India Act 1919. The sole purpose of this Act was to ensure Indians their representation in the government.
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
The main features of these reforms were:
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms

Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms

Bicameral legislature was introduced at the center. • The provincial governments were given more powers. • Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces. • Principle of direct elections with communal electorates was proposed. • The councils were given large powers of legislation. • The right to vote was severely restricted. • After ten years a commission will assess the reforms for improvement.
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms

The reforms came with widespread discontent in the country. Both the leading parties rejected the reforms and demanded effective self-government. In March 1919, the British Government introduced the most controversial, hated, and repressive Rowlatt Act. This resulted in protest and violence across India.
Jallianwala Bagh Incident

To control protests government had banned all public gatherings. On 13 April 1913, the day of "Baisakhi" people gathered in Jallianwala Bagh Amritsar in Indian Punjab. Seeing the gathering as an act of defiance Brigadier-General Reginald, the commander of British Army in India decided to act.
Jallianwala Bagh Incident

Following Dyer's orders troops surrounded the park and opened fire on the unarmed people, killing several hundred and wounding more than thousand. For Indians, the massacre became a byword for colonial injustice and violence.
The Khilafat Movement

The institution of Caliphate (Khilafat) was very important for the Muslims. Since the time of the Pious Caliphate, the Caliph was the symbolic leader of all Muslims worldwide. In the World War I, the Ottoman Caliphate had sided with Germany against the Great Britain and other Allied Forces.
The Khilafat Movement

During the War, the Muslims of the Subcontinent helped the British on the condition that the holy places of Islam would not be attacked, and the institution of Caliphate would not be harmed. After victory, the British Government did not fulfil their promise. The territories of Ottoman Turkey were divided among France, Italy, Greece, and Britain.
The Khilafat Movement

Under great anger and distress, the Muslims of the Subcontinent rose against the British Government and started a mass movement called the Khilafat Movement. The aims of this movement were to protect the holy sites of Islam, to restore the territories of Ottoman Turkey and to restore the Ottoman Caliphate.
The Khilafat Movement
Maulana Muhammad Ali Jauhar and his brother Maulana Shaukat Ali played a significant role as the frontline leaders of this movement.
The Khilafat Movement

During the Khilafat Movement, the Muslims and the Hindus acted together against the common enemy, the British Government. This movement helped bringing both the nations closer to each other and forget their differences temporarily. The movement suffered a big blow when the Hindus withdrew their support in 1922.
The Khilafat Movement
Later, it entirely ended when the caliphate was abolished in March 1924 by the newly founded republic of Turkey under the leadership of Mustafa Kamal Ataturk.

The Khilafat Movement

The Khilafat Movement helped creating political awareness among the Muslims of the Subcontinent. Muslims also realized that the two-nation theory was valid and, despite temporary alliance, a long-term coalition with the Hindus was not possible.
The Khilafat Movement
Despite its failure, the Khilafat Movement inspired the Muslims of the Subcontinent to continue their struggle for independence which gave rise to the Pakistan Movement in later years.
Role of Indians in World War I

During World War-I, July 1914 to Nov. 1918, Subcontinent was the largest British colony. Both the Muslims and the Hindus pledged loyalty to the British in this war. It is estimated that 1.3 million Indian soldiers including the Muslims and Hindus served in World War I and over 74,000 of them sacrificed their lives and a large number were wounded.
Role of Indians in World War I

The British had insincerely promised to deliver progressive self-rule to India at the end of the war. Indian Muslims participated in this war even knowing that Turkey as only surviving Muslim power in the world and seat of "Caliphate".
Role of Indians in World War I

When the war ended with British victory, instead of keeping the pledge, the British imposed the repressive Rowlatt Act. The spirit of loyalty and cooperation showed by Indians in the beginning of war was destroyed at the end of war giving birth to movements such as Civil Disobedience and Khilafat Movement.
Nehru Report

A seven members Statutory Commission, commonly known as the Simon Commission appointed by British Government reached India in 1928. The commission was dispatched to suggest constitutional reforms in India. All the major political parties of Subcontinent boycotted the commission as it did not include any Indian. Finding no alternative, the government asked Indians to draft proposals for forthcoming constitution.
Nehru Report
Indian leaders accepted the offer held All Parties Conference in Delhi.
Nehru Report
A committee headed by Motilal Nehru was assigned the task to draft proposed constitution. The main recommendations of committee commonly known as Nehru Report were as follows:
Nehru Report

India should be given Dominion status. This means independence within the British Commonwealth. • India should be a federation which with a bicameral legislature at the Centre. • Governor General of India would be the constitutional head of India and will have the same powers as that of British Crown. • There will be no separate electorate for minorities. • There should be 1/4th Muslim Representation at Centre.
Nehru Report
• System of weightage should not be adopted for any province.
Nehru Report

The Muslims rejected the report. According to them it was reversal of Lucknow Pact. Quaid-e-Azam representing the Muslim League demanded amendments in the report which were rejected by the Congress. He considered it as the parting of the ways.
Fourteen Points of Quaid-e-Azam

After approval of Nehru Report by Congress Quaid-e-Azam was convinced that the Hindu mindset in India was depriving the Indian Muslims of their rights. To safeguard the rights of Muslims, he was authorized to draft the proposals for future constitution. He presented these proposals at annual session of All India Muslim League held in March 1929.
Fourteen Points of Quaid-e-Azam
These demands were fourteen in numbers so they came to be known as Jinnah's Fourteen Points.
Fourteen Points of Quaid-e-Azam

The council of All India Muslim League accepted these demands through a resolution. The resolution said that no scheme for future constitution would be acceptable for the Muslims of Subcontinent until and unless the demands of Muslims in form of Jinnah's Fourteen Points are incorporated in it.

Self-government within the British Empire, or without the British Empire, the formation of a consolidated North-Western Indian Muslim State appears to me to be the final destiny of the Muslims at least of North-West India".

Allahabad Address 1930

Allama Iqbal maintained that Muslims were not a minority but a community and a nation with civic significance with different, distinct and an exclusive identity. The foundational demand was the right for self-governance for Muslims of India.
Allahabad Address 1930

The most impactful outcome of Allama Iqbal's Allahabad address was that it answered the 'identity question' for Muslims and washed all political confusions from the minds of the Muslims thus shaping and uniting the struggle of Muslims for separate homeland.

Round Table Conferences

Indian political community showed great resentment over Simon Commission Report. Congress launched Civil Disobedience Movement. Muslims rejected the report and demanded consultations with all communities in India. In wake of increasing frustration among Indian masses, the British Government decided to hold talks with Indian regarding constitutional reforms.
Round Table Conferences

For these three rounds of consultation and discussion were held in London from 1930 to 1932 commonly known as Round Table Conferences. First round of conference could not bear any result as Congress leadership did not participate. Second Round Table Conference failed due to unrealistic stance of Gandhi that he represents all the Indians. Congress remained absent in 3rd Conference.
Round Table Conferences
The recommendations were published by the government in 1933 in the form of White Paper later discussed in the British Parliament. Government of India Act 1935 based on these recommendations.
Round Table Conferences
Figure: Round Table Conference in London.
Communal Award

The Indian Councils Act 1909 established separate electorate for Muslims, which was later expanded to include Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans by the Government of India Act 1919. However, Depressed Classes (Dalits) were not granted this right. Simon Commission recommended reserved seats for them instead of separate electorate.
Communal Award

Representatives of Depressed Classes were invited in Round Table Conferences to discuss their stance. 1st and 2nd Round Table Conference failed to resolve the issue as Congress refused separate electorate for Depressed Classes. Finding no way, the British Government announced its own formula in 1932 known as "Communal Award". This award retained separate electorate for Muslims and all other minorities in India.
Communal Award
Based on weightage Muslim received more representation in Muslim minority provinces.

The Indian Elections 1937

In 1937, the elections for eleven provincial assemblies were held under the Indian Government Act 1935. Out of 1585 seats, the Indian National Congress won 706 while the Muslim League won 106 seats. Hence, the Congress could not prove its point of being the sole representative of the people of India. In July 1937, the Congress ministries were formed.
The Congress Ministries

Even though the Muslim League offered the Indian National Congress to form a coalition government, the Congress refused the offer. For the next two years, the Congress Ministries mainly worked for asserting the Hindu supremacy. Hindi was declared as the national language. Anti-Muslim educational reforms were introduced to displace the two-nation theory from the minds of the Muslims.
The Congress Ministries
Some Congress leaders claimed these steps as revenging the previous 700-year Muslim rule over them.
The Congress Ministries

To investigate and voice atrocities and injustice committed by Congress ministries, the Council of All India Muslim League appointed an eight-member committee under the presidentship of Raja Syed Muhammad Mehdi of Pirpur. The committee presented its report on November 15, 1938.
The Congress Ministries
Pirpur and other reports of similar nature played an important role to awaken the Muslims to be united under the flag of All India Muslim League.
The Congress Ministries

In September 1939, the Second World War started, and the Congress refused to cooperate with the British against the Germans and their allies. Under those circumstances, the Congress Ministries resigned. Hence, a period of atrocities for the Muslims came to an end. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah announced December 22, 1939, as the 'Day of Deliverance'.
Let us think
Attitude of Congress leadership towards Muslims and minorities led to partition of India. Do you think that situation has not changed in India for minorities?
Reorganization of All India Muslim League

Advocate of Hindu Muslim unity, Muhammad Ali Jinnah was completely disappointed by anti-Muslim attitude of Hindu leaders reflected in Nehru Report. Situation within Muslim League saddened him further. After attending First Round Table Conference he decided to leave India and settle down in London.
Reorganization of All India Muslim League

In 1933 proposal of separate Muslim state with name of Pakistan motivated young Muslim intellectuals in India to accelerate political consciousness. After correspondence with Allama Muhammad Iqbal, Muhammad Ali Jinnah realized that organizing the Muslims of India into one powerful and dynamic organization was badly needed and that it is not an easy task.
Reorganization of All India Muslim League
He came back to India in 1934 with the aim to work for the betterment of Indian Muslims.
Reorganization of All India Muslim League

He had to unite Muslim league as sole representative of Muslims of India. As president of Muslim League, he moved to reorganize the party making it popular among ordinary Muslims. Muslim League could not perform well in 1937 Elections. Congress ministries made it a bit easier to unite the Muslims on League's platform.

As a results of Quaid's dedication and untiring efforts Muslim League emerged as representative of Indian Muslims in 1940.

The Lahore Resolution

The Lahore Resolution is considered as a landmark document in the history of Pakistan. The All India Muslim League held its 27th Annual General Session between March 22 and 24 at Iqbal Park, Lahore. On March 23, 1940, this historical resolution, which was first called the Lahore Resolution and in the later years known as the Pakistan Resolution, was presented.
The Lahore Resolution

A monument called 'Minar-e-Pakistan' stands in Lahore in honor of this famous resolution. March 23 is observed as a national holiday in Pakistan to celebrate the Republic Day and to commemorate the Lahore Resolution.
Quaid-e-Azam's Address

On the first day of the session, Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah delivered a speech saying that the Hindus and the Muslims were two different nations, deriving their inspiration from different sources and personalities. He said, "Mussalmans are a nation according to any definition of a nationhood.
Quaid-e-Azam's Address

We wish our people to develop to the fullest spiritual, cultural, economic, social and political life in a way that we think best and in consonance with our own ideals and according to the genius of our people".

The Resolution
On March 23, 1940, A. K. Fazl ul Haq, then the Chief Minister of the Bengal province, moved the resolution in the general session, which was called the 'Lahore Resolution.' The resolution said:
The Resolution

"That the areas in which Muslims are numerically in majority as in the North-Western and Eastern zones of India should be grouped to constitute independent states in which the constituent units shall be autonomous and sovereign."
The Resolution

The resolution was seconded by Chaudhry Khaliquzzaman. Later, Maulana Zafar Ali Khan from Punjab, Sir Abdullah Haroon from Sindh, Qazi Muhammad Esa from Balochistan and Sardar Aurangzeb from North-West Frontier Province (Now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) extended their support to the Resolution.

Significance of the Lahore Resolution

The Lahore Resolution (later called the Pakistan Resolution) is the most important milestone during the struggle for Pakistan. This resolution made it clear that there was only one destination for the Muslims of the Subcontinent: Pakistan. Earlier, there was a demand for the separate electorate. Muslims then voiced their demand for a separate (continued on the next page)

state. Both the British and the Hindus rejected this resolution which placed the Muslims under the leadership of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

The Lahore Resolution was passed on March 24, 1940 but the Pakistan Day is celebrated on March 23rd. It is because this landmark resolution was presented to the Annual General Session of All India Muslim League on March 23, 1940.
Success of the Muslim League in the 1945-46 Elections

Another important landmark in Pakistan's struggle is the 1945-46 elections. On August 21, 1945, Viceroy Lord Wavell announced that the elections to the central and provincial assemblies would be held. This signed a major change in the policies of the new British Government that came into power after the Second World War.
Success of the Muslim League in the 1945-46 Elections

In the 1937 elections, the Muslims of the Subcontinent did not know how cruel the Congress Ministries would be. Between 1937 and 1939, the Congress Ministries proved to be a nightmare for the Muslims. The 1945-46 elections were not less than a referendum for Pakistan. The Muslim League participated in these elections in the name of Pakistan as a sovereign country for the Muslims of the Subcontinent.
Success of the Muslim League in the 1945-46 Elections
Quaid-e-Azam and the other leaders of the Muslim League speeded their efforts to make the elections a success for the Muslims.
Success of the Muslim League in the 1945-46 Elections

In next few weeks, despite his health issues, Quaid-e-Azam addressed thousand of peoples. He spoke at many gatherings in different provinces, issued press statements and gave interviews. The elections for the central assembly were held in December 1945. The Muslim League showed impressive performance and won all 30 reserved seats for the Muslims.
Success of the Muslim League in the 1945-46 Elections

For the provincial assemblies, the elections were conducted in January 1946 where the Muslim League won about 95% of the total Muslim seats. These results were a clear proof that the Muslim League was the sole representative of the Muslims of the Subcontinent. After this clear verdict, the emergence of Pakistan became more obvious than before.
Success of the Muslim League in the 1945-46 Elections
An interim government was formed until the independence of Pakistan and India. This government helped the British Government in the process of transferring the power to the local people.
The 3rd June Plan

In next few months, the Congress also realized that it was no longer possible to avoid the partition of the country into two sovereign states. On June 3, 1947, the British Prime Minister Atlee announced the Partition Plan, which is also known as the 3rd June Plan.
The 3rd June Plan

According to the plan, the provincial assemblies of Bengal and Punjab would meet in two parts separately to vote the decision on partition. The provincial assemblies of Sindh and Balochistan were authorized to express their own decisions. In the North-West Frontier Province (NWFP), the partition decision was to be taken through a referendum. Similarly, a referendum was to be held in Sylhet region of Assam.
The 3rd June Plan
The princely states were not to be transferred to either India or Pakistan before their own decision.
The Indian Independence Act
On the basis of June 3 Plan, the Indian Independence Act was passed by the British Parliament in July 1947.
The Indian Independence Act
The following are the salient features of this Act:
The Indian Independence Act

The Indian Independence Act

On August 15, India would be divided into two dominion states: Pakistan and India. • The boundaries between the two states were to be determined by a Boundary Commission called the Radcliffe Commission. • Punjab was to be divided into two parts i.e., East Punjab and West Punjab. Similarly, Bengal was also to be divided into East and West Bengal.
The Indian Independence Act

• Pakistan was to comprise the West Punjab, East Bengal, Sindh, North-West Frontier Province (NWFP), and Balochistan. • The princely states were free to join either India or Pakistan or remain independent. • For the time being till the constitution was made, both of them would be governed in accordance with the Government of India Act 1935.

The Creation of Pakistan

Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah went to Karachi where the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan met on August 11, 1947. After three days, he took oath as the Governor General of Pakistan. On the midnight connecting August 14 and 15, 1947, Pakistan came into existence as a sovereign Muslim state. Karachi was declared as the capital of Pakistan.
The Creation of Pakistan

• The seeds of independence that had been sowed through the War of Independence in 1857 bore fruit in 1947. The Muslims of the Subcontinent won this battle through ballot and legal means under the dynamic leadership of Quaid-e-Azam. Transition, however, could not remain smooth. Millions of people from both sides of the border had to move to their new countries.
The Creation of Pakistan

Hundreds and thousands of Muslims lost their lives on their way to Pakistan. • It is our earnest responsibility to work hard to uphold our country in line with the aspirations of Allama Iqbal and Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

Muslims ruled Subcontinent for more than one thousand year. During this time, despite various religious differences, the people enjoyed peace and harmony. Other religions got their due right during different regimes. In 18th century British came into power and after unsuccessful War of Independence in 1857, Muslims rule in this region came to an end.

Creation of Pakistan

Pakistan came into being after a long struggle. This struggle was aimed at achieving a separate state for the Muslims where Islamic principles could be exercised without any fear. This was a legal and political struggle under the dynamic leadership of Quaid-e-Azam (continued on the next page)

Major Problems for Pakistan at the Time of Independence

Lahore Resolution on 23rd March 1940 was a great milestone of this struggle when the Muslims asked for a separate independent state consisting majority Muslim areas, where they could spend their life according to their beliefs. This resolution was later called as Pakistan Resolution and today 23rd March is celebrated as Pakistan Day.
Major Problems for Pakistan at the Time of Independence

Though this struggle was based on legal grounds, the transition could not remain peaceful. After announcement of independence by the British, and especially after the creation of Pakistan on 14th August 1947, people faced bloodshed while travelling to other side of the border. Migration of millions of people and their settlement in newly formed state was one of the immediate problems.
Major Problems for Pakistan at the Time of Independence
However, there were certain other issues that Pakistan had to face right from its inception in August 1947.
Major Problems for Pakistan at the Time of Independence
Right after independence, Pakistan had to face certain issues which needed quick resolution. Following are some of the problems:
Major Problems for Pakistan at the Time of Independence
Geographical Problems: Two wings of Pakistan; East Pakistan and West Pakistan were separated by about 1000 miles of Indian land.
Major Problems for Pakistan at the Time of Independence
Economic Problems: Pakistan was made up of mainly underdeveloped states with around 90% of rural population. Hardly 10% of industrial enterprises came in Pakistan's share.

Major Problems for Pakistan at the Time of Independence

Long struggle of the Muslims of the Subcontinent resulted in an independent country Pakistan. It was a great reward for their efforts but early period of this newborn nation brought many challenges. Their resolution was very important as they were a danger for the very existence of Pakistan.

The most important of Indo-Pakistan disputes was the question of sharing the waters of the Indus basin. Due to unjust boundary distribution India got hold of the basins of the rivers. problem Pakistani Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan and Indian Prime Minister Jawahar Lal Nehru signed and agreement on 8th April 1952. This pact was called "Liaquat-Nehru Pact". This pact provided rights to the minorities to both sides.
Objectives Resolution

At the time of independence, with some amendments, Indian Act 1935 and Freedom of India Act 1947, were enforced as the constitution of Pakistan. However, there was a great need for the new constitution of this independent country. For this reason, efforts were started from the beginning, though they could not bear fruit till 1956.
Objectives Resolution

Objectives Resolution was one of the early efforts, directed towards development of new constitution of Pakistan. This resolution was moved by the first Prime Minister of Pakistan, Liaqat Ali Khan. The first constituent assembly of Pakistan deliberated this resolution in detail and adopted this on March 12, 1949.
Objectives Resolution
Liaqat Ali Khan termed the passage of the Objectives Resolution as "the most important occasion in the history of Pakistan, next in importance only to the achievement of independence."
Principles of Objectives Resolution

As per the prescribed principles for development of constitution, it was declared that sovereignty over the entire universe belongs to Almighty Allah alone. It was further emphasized that the authority given by Allah to the state of Pakistan through its people is a sacred trust, thus it is to be exercised within the limits prescribed by Him.
Importance of Objectives Resolution

This Resolution reinforces the concept of the sovereignty of Allah. It emphasizes the political philosophy of Islam that only Allah Almighty is the source of authority for the whole Universe. This ideology is different from the philosophy of western democracy that emphasizes that sovereignty lies in the people.
Importance of Objectives Resolution
Objectives Resolution clarified that people would utilize powers entrusted by Allah within the limits prescribed by Him.
Importance of Objectives Resolution

This Resolution was important in a way that all the constitutions of Pakistan recognized its principles. In fact, this sentence that the sovereignty belongs to Almighty Allah is incorporated in all the constitutions of Pakistan.
Policy Making in Pakistan

After dealing with initial problems of settling the migrants and unjust division of assets, Pakistan started developing in different areas. May it be foreign policy of Pakistan or internal security, economic policies or health and education, different governments kept striving to bring prosperity to the nation.
Foreign Policy of Pakistan

A foreign policy is a set of plans and schemes to manage a country's relationships with other countries. They are guidelines to regulate international dealings. These policies have different purposes depending upon the interest of a country. These may be developed on the basis of ideologies. In the modern world, they are mostly based on economic interests of the country.
Foreign Policy of Pakistan

Pakistani foreign policy witnessed many ups and downs during the period 1956 to 1977. 1950s was the time of pacts and alliances with the west. Pakistan signed Mutual Defense Assistance Agreement with USA and then South East Asian Treaty Organization or SEATO pact in 1954. In 1955 Pakistan signed another pact that was initially called Baghdad Pact and later called Central Treaty Organization or CENTO.
Foreign Policy of Pakistan
This pact was designed to strengthen the nations in the region.
Foreign Policy of Pakistan

During this time, Pakistan fought two wars against India, first in 1965 and then in 1971. Kashmir issue remained the flash point of relations between Pakistan and India. The climax of Pakistan's relations with Islamic countries was 2nd summit of Organization of Islamic Countries (OIC) in Lahore in 1974.

Foreign Policy of Pakistan

Constitution

Constitution is the body of policies and practices that form the essential organizing principle of a state. In some cases, such as Pakistan, the constitution is a specific written document; in others, such as the United Kingdom, it is a collection of documents, laws, and traditional practices that are generally accepted as governing political matters.
Importance of Constitution

It is the constitution of a country that binds all the people together without considering their faith, colour, race or socio-economic background. It is not possible for any individual, organization or even government to know everything in order to ensure the safety and happiness of the people. The constitution recognizes this, and therefore guarantees the rights of citizens.
Importance of Constitution
No law or order of the government can violate the constitution. Constitution is the supreme law, and all institutions are bound to follow it.
Important Constitutional Terminology

Bill: A Bill is a draft of proposed law. It is presented to the parliament for discussion. After discussion, bill may be passed or rejected. • Act: When a bill is passed by parliament, it becomes Act. Once a bill becomes act, it cannot be changed easily. • Law: Law is a set of regulations or rules to be followed. Anything which has the power to confer legal rights, obligations, liabilities, etc are laws. • Amendment:
Important Constitutional Terminology
Constitutional amendment means any modification, deletion, or additions made to the constitution. • Ordinance: Ordinances are temporary laws that are circulated by the President.
Constitutions in Pakistan

At the time of independence of Pakistan, Government of India Act, 1935 was adopted as constitution of the newly established state. However, it was necessary to make Pakistan's own constitution which could provide guideline to run the affairs of the nation. Unfortunately, for the first few years no constitution could be made. Later, three constitutions were made in different years.
Constitutions in Pakistan
Constitutions of Pakistan: 1956, 1962, 1973.
1956 Constitution

In 1956, the new assembly adopted the country's first constitution. It was a constitution with 234 articles, divided into 13 parts. According to this constitution, the country was declared as an Islamic State. Federal System was announced with division of powers mentioned. Under the constitution parliamentary form of government was adopted.
1956 Constitution
In the constitution of 1956, both Urdu and Bengali were made official languages of Pakistan. English was accepted as official language for a period of 25 years.
1956 Constitution
Unfortunately, this constitution lasted only for two years. In 1958 General Muhammad Ayub Khan dissolved the assembly and imposed first Martial Law in the country.
1956 Constitution
After waiting for a couple of years, Ayub Khan started making efforts for a new constitution, on 8th June 1962, new constitution of the country was enacted.
1962 Constitution
Salient features of the 1962 constitution are as under:
1962 Constitution

This constitution consisted of 250 articles. • Presidential form of government was introduced. President was to be elected indirectly by 80,000 Basic Democracy members. • A federal system was introduced in the country. It consisted of a central government and two provincial governments comprising in East and West Pakistan. Provincial government was headed by a governor.
1962 Constitution

• No Law could be passed against the teachings of Quran and Sunnah. • Fundamental Rights including rights of speech and expression, freedom to choose profession and freedom to profess religion were assured without any discrimination.
1973 Constitution

The first two constitutions of Pakistan could not stay long and there was a need of a constitution that could provide long term solution. As a result of hard work of democratic forces all the leaders in the assembly signed the draft of 1973 constitution. After approval from both houses, the 1973 constitution was enforced on 14th August 1973.
Salient Features of the 1973 Constitution

This constitution consists of 12 parts and 280 articles. • Islam is declared as the state religion and Objectives Resolution was made part of the constitution. • In order to make any amendment in the constitution two-third majority of the parliament is necessary. • Islamic provisions have been included in this constitution.
Salient Features of the 1973 Constitution

• Federal system was introduced in the constitution with a central government and four provincial governments. President is the head of the state who is elected by the members of all the assemblies. • Parliamentary form of government was introduced in which Prime Minister is the head of the government. Prime Minister is elected by the members of the National Assembly. • Parliament consists of two houses.
Salient Features of the 1973 Constitution

Senate is the upper house whereas National Assembly is the lower house. • Unlike 1962 constitution, direct method of election was adopted. • Fundamental rights of the people are ensured including article 25-A that makes the state responsible for providing free education to all children between the ages of 6 to 15 years. • Judiciary was made independent.
Human Rights Guaranteed in the 1973 Constitution
Freedom of speech • Freedom of movement • Freedom of assembly • Right to vote • Right to security • Freedom of religion • Right to education • Right to own property • Equality as a citizen
Note for Teachers

Ask the students to learn more about human rights guaranteed in the constitution of Pakistan. Among these rights, an important part is right to education. Constitutional Amendments

Constitution of Pakistan provides solution to almost all the issues related to governance. However, in later years, different constitutional amendments were made in the constitution. Through these amendments different articles of the constitutions were amended or new articles were introduced.
Constitutional Amendments

Through eighth amendment in 1985 the President of Pakistan was given authority to dissolve the assemblies. This amendment was introduced in 1985 by the assembly elected through non-party elections. This power of dissolution of assemblies by the President and the provincial governors was taken back through thirteenth amendment in 1997.
Constitutional Amendments
This power of dissolution of assemblies by the President was restored again through seventeenth amendment in 2003. It empowered the president once again.
Constitutional Amendments

Eighteenth Constitutional amendment in 2010 was aimed at bringing back the parliamentary supremacy. It gave more powers to the provinces to utilize their resources. In addition this amendment ensured judicial autonomy, removed discretionary powers of the President of Pakistan and improved the situation of women empowerment through introduction of 5% quota for women in election tickets by the political parties.
Kashmir Conflict

According to the partition plan of the Subcontinent, the areas of Muslim majorities were added to Pakistan while those with Hindu majority went with India. Princely states were given authority to choose their destiny as per the wishes of their people.
Kashmir Conflict

Under this formula many states including Bahawalpur, Swat, Khairpur, Lasbela, Kharan, Makran and others joined Pakistan after partition. Kashmir was also an independent state with 80% Muslim population. The people of Kashmir also demanded to join Pakistan.
Kashmir Conflict

However, against the wishes of people and surrendering to Indian pressure, the Dogra Raja of Kashmir, agreed to join India by signing the controversial Instrument of Accession on 26th October 1947. Indian Governor General, Lord Mountbatten provisionally accepted Kashmir into Indian Union.
Kashmir Conflict

In the letter to the Maharaja on 27 October 1947, Mountbatten made it clear that the State would only be incorporated into the Indian Union after a reference had been made to the people of Kashmir. In this way India accepted the rule of referendum but always negated it. In such circumstances, in 1947, first Pak-India war started over the issue of Kashmir.
Kashmir Conflict
After start of the war, India took the issue to United Nations. In 1949, the UN announced ceasefire between the two countries. This ceasefire line is called the Line of Control.
Kashmir Conflict
At this stage it is necessary to understand the difference between line of control and international borders.
Line of Control (LoC)

The term Line of Control (LoC) refers to the military control line between the Indian and Pakistani-controlled parts of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. This line is considered as the de facto border.
Line of Control (LoC)
The total length of Line of Control is 740 km or 460 miles.
International Border

International Border is the border that determines the territory of a country that is recognized by the world. The International Border (IB) is the India-Pakistan Border which serves as a border between the countries of India and Pakistan. This is the official international border that is recognized by the world. Its total length is 2900 km.
International Border
This is based on Radcliffe line which was published on 17th August 1947 as a boundary demarcation line between India and Pakistan upon the Partition of India.
UN Resolution Regarding Kashmir
After the 1947-48 war, United Nations passed several resolutions to solve this issue of Kashmir. The United Nations Security Council Resolution of 21st April 1948 stated that,
UN Resolution Regarding Kashmir
"both India and Pakistan desire that the question of the accession of Jammu and Kashmir to India or Pakistan should be decided through the democratic method of a free and impartial plebiscite".
UN Resolution Regarding Kashmir

Subsequent UN Security Council (UNSC) resolutions reiterated the same stand. In addition to security council the UN Commission for India and Pakistan (UNCIP) resolutions of 3rd August 1948 and 5th January 1949 reinforced UNSC resolutions.
UN Resolution Regarding Kashmir

Other Border Disputes
As the Indian governments did not act upon UN resolutions, Kashmiri people started struggle for self-determination. Thousands of men, women and children have lost their lives to achieve their goal.
Other Border Disputes

Kashmir issue is not only a humanitarian problem for the people of Kashmir but also a great threat for the world peace. Both Pakistan and India are atomic powers, and any mishandling may lead to great devastation. The solution to the dispute requires a referendum for the whole of Jammu & Kashmir under international auspices.
Other Border Disputes
UN resolutions call for the holding of a referendum to determine the wishes of the Kashmiri people.
Other Border Disputes
In addition to Kashmir conflict, there are some other border conflicts between Pakistan and India. Most important of these are Siachen and Sir Creek.
Siachen Conflict

Siachen glacier is one of the largest glaciers of the world, situated in Himalayas. Since the border was not clear in this region, India launched an operation to capture all the Siachen Glacier in 1984. Pakistan also sent its forces to oust India from this area. Since then, Siachen is the world's highest and probably the most expensive war front.
Sir Creek

This is a maritime boundary line between Kutch and Sindh. Before partition, this region was a part of Bombay Presidency but after independence in 1947, Sindh became a part of Pakistan while Kutch became a part of India. Since then it became a dispute between Pakistan and India. This strip of 60 miles is important because of oil and gas resources. That is the reason India has been claiming this Pakistani land.
Sir Creek
Despite many efforts, this issue is still unresolved.
Armed Conflicts

Due to these border conflicts and specially because of Kashmir Issue, Pakistani and Indian armed forces came face to face in war ground time and again. First limited war was fought soon after independence in 1948. The second was 1965 followed by 1971 and another limited scale conflict in 1998 at Kargil.
1948 War

As mentioned earlier, when Maharaja of Kashmir Hari Singh, decided to join India despite clear Muslim majority, the tribal people from Kashmir tried to gain their land with power in October 1947. They captured many areas and reached near the capital Srinagar when Indian forces came to help forces of Maharaja of Kashmir.
1948 War
Pakistani Chief of Army, General Douglas Gracey did not send Pakistani forces despite orders from Quaid-e-Azam.
1948 War

Despite this the brave tribal forces captured a significant part of Kashmir. At that moment India took this issue into United Nations which helped announce ceasefire. This military ceasefire line became Line of Control that divides Indian Occupied Kashmir and Azad Jammu & Kashmir.
1948 War

United Nations passed resolutions to solve the issue of Kashmir as per the wishes of Kashmiris, but India avoided it, so the problem remained unsolved. This caused another armed conflict in the shape of Indo-Pak War 1965.
1965 War

In April 1965, Indian forces intruded into Pakistani area in the Rann of Kutch. In a sharp but short conflict, the Indian forces were evicted by Pakistan Army. Later, an international tribunal gave verdict in favour of Pakistan. In these circumstances, Indian leadership started planning to occupy Azad Kashmir.
1965 War
Figure: Squadron Leader M. M. Alam; The hero of Pakistan during 1965 war.
1965 War

In the wake of these operations against India in Rann of Kutch, Pakistan government decided to launch a guerrilla operation with the title 'Operation Gibraltar' in Indian illegally occupied Kashmir. The operation was aimed at bringing Kashmir issue into prominence which was getting into oblivion.
1965 War

The Indian Army responded to this operation by launching a full-scale war on international borders on 6th September 1965. Initially, Indian Army crossed the international border and attacked Lahore and Kasur fronts, but gallant Pakistani soldiers stopped the enemy with their will and determination.
1965 War

On 7th September 1965, Pakistani Air Force not only bombarded important Air Bases of India but also destroyed many of their planes during air combat. On the same day Pakistani pilot Squadron Leader M.M.Alam made a world record when he shot down five attacking Indian Air Force aircrafts in a single sortie.
1965 War

Pakistan Navy also played significant role in this war. On 7th September 1965, Pakistan Navy ships bombarded Indian town and radar station Dwarka. Pakistan Navy submarine Ghazi kept the Indian Navy's aircraft carrier besieged in the harbour throughout the war.
1965 War
A memorable battle of tanks was fought on Chwinda (Sialkot) sector where valiant Pakistani soldiers made that place a graveyard of Indian tanks. It is the largest tank battle since World War II.
1965 War
Figure: Huge number of Indian Tanks Destroyed during Battle of Chwinda.
1965 War

After 17 days of war which caused thousands of casualties, the United Nations helped conducting peace talks between the two neighbours. In January 1966, India and Pakistan signed the Tashkent Declaration. In this peace treaty, they agreed to return conquered territories, remove troops, and return to the borders established in 1949.
1965 War

Indo-Pak war of 1965 is one of the most important events of history of Pakistan. The way Pakistani armed forces defended their motherland proves that it is unity, faith and discipline that counts and not the number of armed forces or quality of weapons.
1965 War
Although the Tashkent Agreement achieved its short-term aims, conflict in South Asia reignited a few years later in the shape of 1971 Indo-Pak War.
1971 War
Roots of this war can be traced from geographical, linguistic and economic divide between the two wings of the country: East and West Pakistan.
1971 War

One of the basic issues was language. Bengali was the most spoken language in East Pakistan while Urdu was declared as the National Language of the country. Though in the constitution of 1956, both Urdu and Bengali were declared as national languages, mostly our leadership failed to appreciate the importance of Bengali.
1971 War

Moreover, a perception about economic disparity between the two wings of the country left the people of East Pakistan disillusioned. Though government of Pakistan made some efforts to uplift the economic condition, it was not enough.
1971 War
The main role behind the tragedy of separation of East Pakistan was played by the (continued on the next page)

leadership of both the wings when neither the results of 1971 elections were honoured nor any flexibility was shown from either side. The negative role of foreign media was another important factor which painted a gloomy picture of the situation in East Pakistan.
1971 War

After 1971 elections, taking full advantage of the political crisis between East and West Pakistan, India extended full support to the anti-Pakistan elements in East Pakistan known as Mukti Bahani. In November 1971, Indian forces entered East Pakistan and started attacking Pakistani posts with the help of Mukti Bahani.
1971 War

Tens of thousands of Urdu speaking Biharis, loyal Bengalis and West Pakistani civilians working in East Pakistan were mercilessly killed by Mukti Bahani and other Indian agents, firstly during March 1971 and then after 16th December 1971 which continued till 1972. This was an open and hegemonic Indian aggression against the sovereignty of Pakistan.
1971 War

In order to restore law and order in the country, Pakistani civil administration and armed forces made all possible efforts. Sadly, exaggerated allegations of mass killings and dishonouring of women were levelled against Pakistani forces which were considered false by some international scholars.
1971 War

On 3rd December 1971, war opened on Western Front as well with several Indian attempts to cross the international border. Pakistani forces fought heroically, and Indian forces were defeated on many fronts.
1971 War
Meanwhile peace efforts were initiated by United Nations which could not be materialized due to disagreement between other members of UN Security Council.
1971 War

One of the most significant heroes of this war is Major Muhammad Akram Shaheed. During this war, the company of Major Muhammad Akram Shaheed came under heavy air, artillery, and armor attacks. Despite enemy's superiority in numbers and ammunition, Major Akram and his soldiers repulsed every attack for two weeks inflicting heavy casualties on the enemy.
1971 War
Major Akram got martyred during this battle and was crowned with the highest military award in Pakistan: Nishan e Haider.
1971 War
Figure: Major Muhammad Akram Shaheed.
1971 War

On 9th December Pakistani Submarine Hangor, under the command of Commander Ahmad Tasnim, intercepted Indian Navy Ships Khukri and Kirpan. Commander Ahmed Tasnim rendered heroic services during 1965 war as 2nd in command of Pakistan Navy Submarine 'Ghazi'.

1971 War

In this spectacular action which took place about 30 miles south off the Indian Kathiawar Coast, the submarine delivered successful attacks on both the ships, as a result of which Indian Navy Ship Khukri sank within two minutes of receiving a torpedo. Another torpedo hit Kirpan was severely damaged. This came as a shattering blow to the Indian Navy.
1971 War

This was the first time after World War II in which a submarine had sunk an enemy warship in a naval engagement. Vice Admiral Ahmad Tasnim is distinctly decorated with Sitara-e-Jurrat conferred upon him twice for his actions of valour in 1965 and 1971 wars.
1971 War

Pakistani forces fought gallantly and offered supreme sacrifices for the defence of country. However, faced with heavy odds and surrounded by Indian forces and Mukti Bahini on three sides and Bay of Bengal on one side Pakistani armed forces had no option but to lay down arms on 16 December 1971 to stop further bloodshed of civil population of East Pakistan. This gave birth to a new state Bangladesh.
1971 War

Pakistani forces numbering about 35,000 to 40,000 along with civil officials and their families totalling about 93,000 became prisoners of war. They were repatriated to Pakistan in 1974 under Delhi Agreement of 1973.
1971 War

The main lesson of 1971 tragedy is that we should learn to accept and appreciate the diversity within the country. People should be given their rights as outlined in the constitution of Pakistan. Such tragic events also remind us to keep the spirit of nationhood above and beyond personal and political gains.

Governance in Pakistan

Pakistani nation was very lucky that it got a great leader in shape of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Moreover, the first Prime Minister of Pakistan Liaquat Ali Khan was also a man of great credentials.
Governments in Pakistan from 1947 to 1977

After demise of Quaid-e-Azam and unfortunate assassination of Liaquat Ali Khan, Pakistan could not see any long-lasting government and in very few years many Presidents and Prime Ministers came and went. Following is the list of Governor Generals, Presidents, and Prime Ministers of Pakistan during this period:

During this period, he was able to face early challenges of Pakistan with his unmatched leadership skills. During the period of Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan, Liaquat-Nehru Pact was signed. Moreover, Objectives Resolution was also passed.

Liaquat Ali Khan was assassinated on October 16, 1951.
Rulers 1947–1977
In 1956 first constitution of Pakistan was promulgated in which Pakistan was declared a Federal Islamic Republic.
General Muhammad Ayub Khan (1958 to 1969)

In 1958, General Muhammad Ayub Khan imposed Martial Law in the country. Through promulgation of the new constitution in 1962, Ayub Khan introduced a local government system with the title of Basic Democracies. Later, the representatives of the local governments elected Ayub Khan as president of Pakistan.
General Muhammad Ayub Khan (1958 to 1969)

Ten years rule of Ayub Khan is labelled as the 'decade of development'. Agricultural, industrial, social, and educational reforms were the highlights of this period. Three major dams were built to help agriculture and provision of cost-effective energy for Pakistan. In 1965, Pakistan faced a seventeen days' long war against India. In 1967, capital of Pakistan was shifted from Karachi to a newly built city Islamabad.
General Muhammad Ayub Khan (1958 to 1969)

General Muhammad Ayub Khan (1958 to 1969)

Due to political unrest, Ayub Khan stepped down and General Yahya Khan became the new president of Pakistan in March 1969. General elections were held in 1970 which caused more unrest which resulted in separation of East Pakistan as a new country Bangladesh.
Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto (1971 to 1977)

Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto served as President of Pakistan between 1971 and 1973. Later, he took oath as the Prime Minister after promulgation of the 1973 constitution of Pakistan. Simla Agreement with India, promulgation of unanimously passed Constitution in 1973, nationalization of industries, and rehabilitation of a war-ridden country were few of the highlights of his era.
Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto (1971 to 1977)

Land reforms, labour reforms, administrative reforms, education, health, and social reforms were introduced during this period. Moreover, Pakistan started its nuclear program which helped Pakistan gain strategic deterrence.
Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto (1971 to 1977)

After an early election in 1977, political unrest spread across the country. On July 5, 1977, Chief of Army Staff General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq imposed martial law in the country.
Pakistani Governments after 1977
The period between 1977 and 2020 can be divided into following four phases:
Pakistani Governments after 1977
General Zia ul Haq: 1977 to 1988

On 5th July 1977, General Zia-ul-Haq imposed martial law in the country. For the next 11 years, he remained the Head of State. He promised to hold elections within 90 days but this was postponed. Later, in 1979, many political leaders were disqualified, and elections were again postponed for uncertain period.
General Zia ul Haq: 1977 to 1988

In 1984, a referendum was held as a result of which, the Chief Martial Law Administrator General Zia-ul-Haq became the President of Pakistan. After the referendum, he announced holding general elections on a non-party basis in February 1985.
General Zia ul Haq: 1977 to 1988

General elections were held on February 25, 1985. Main opposition parties boycotted the elections. As a result of these elections, Muhammad Khan Junejo became the Prime Minister of Pakistan while General Zia-ul-Haq continued as President of Pakistan. On 17th August 1988, General Zia died when his plane mysteriously crashed near Bahawalpur.
General Zia ul Haq: 1977 to 1988

In 1982, General Zia visited China and the Karakorum Highway was inaugurated. Islamization became the main policy during Zia government. During this period, Pakistan continued developing its military might in both conventional as well as non-conventional weapons.
General Zia ul Haq: 1977 to 1988
During the period of General Zia-ul-Haq Soviet Union attacked Afghanistan and millions of Afghan refugees came to Pakistan. Let's learn about Afghan War.
Afghan War

The political, economic, and social conflict between the Soviet Union and the United States and their ideological allies worldwide is termed as cold war. The United States formed the Western Bloc, and the Soviet Union formed the Eastern Bloc. It was a period of tension which started in 1946 between the two countries and lasted for almost half a century.
Afghan War

During this period both the superpowers of the world developed not only conventional weapons but also developed nuclear weaponry. The Cold War reached its climax when the USSR invaded neighbouring country Afghanistan.
Afghan War

The main reason that triggered Afghan War was the murder of Nur Muhammad Tarakai, the then President of Afghanistan. Tarakai was a communist politician who had support of USSR. He was ousted by Hafeezullah Amin who grabbed the power of Afghanistan. Soon after assuming power, Amin started talks with the USA which alarmed USSR.
Afghan War
In these circumstances, USSR invaded Afghanistan in December 1979 when around 80,000 Russian soldiers entered into Afghanistan and installed the government of Babrik Karmil in Kabul.
Afghan War

Pakistan did not accept the foreign aided government as it felt threatened because of the presence of the occupying Soviet forces in the neighbouring country. There was a threat that the Soviet forces would not stay till Afghanistan and would try to enter Pakistani soil in order to reach the warm waters of the Arabian Sea.
Afghan War

USA and the western bloc had their own apprehensions who considered this move of the USSR as the first step in their effort to reach the warm waters. Mujahideen started resistance against the occupying forces through guerilla war. USA and allies supported Mujahideen against their arch enemy USSR. Due to war, some 3 million Afghans became refugees in Pakistan.
Afghan War
As a frontline state in this war, Pakistan received massive military and financial assistance from the United States, but it had to pay the price in the shape of terrorism in the country.
Benazir Bhutto (1988 - 1990)

Benazir Bhutto was the daughter of Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto. After death of Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, she went into exile and came back to Pakistan in 1986. Her political party, Pakistan People's Party (PPP) won general elections in 1988 and she became the first woman Prime Minister of Pakistan and the Islamic World. She lifted ban on students' unions and traders' unions.
Benazir Bhutto (1988 - 1990)

South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) Conference in Pakistan, peace treaties with India and Pakistan's re-joining Commonwealth were the highlights of PPP government. Her government could continue only for 18 months, after which President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the assembly.

As a result of the general elections on October 24, 1990, Islami Jamhoori Ittehad (IJI), an alliance of nine political parties, won the elections and Mian Nawaz Sharif became the new Prime Minister of Pakistan. During his tenure, Nawaz Sharif made efforts to uplift the industrial sector. He initiated projects like Ghazi Barotha and Islamabad-Lahore Motorway. Privatization was another highlight of this era.
Mian Nawaz Sharif (1990 - 1993)
In April 1993, President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the assembly and new elections were held.

As a result of elections in October 1993, Benazir Bhutto came to power once again. Farooq Ahmed Khan Laghari became the new president. During her tenure, Benazir Bhutto remained successful in uplifting the name of Pakistan as an enlightened country. US sanctions against Pakistan were eased as a result of Brown Amendment. Policy of privatization continued during her tenure and foreign investors also got encouragement.
Benazir Bhutto (1993 - 1996)
In 1996, Benazir government was once again removed from power by the president of Pakistan. This time the president was from her own political party; Farooq Laghari.
Mian Nawaz Sharif (1997 - 1999)

As a result of elections in February 1997, Nawaz Sharif became Prime Minister once again and this time with two-third majority. During this term, in 1998, Pakistan conducted nuclear tests. Motorway was also inaugurated during this tenure.
Mian Nawaz Sharif (1997 - 1999)
On October 12, 1999, Nawaz Sharif government was sacked by the Chief of Army Staff General Parvaiz Musharraf who became first, Chief Executive of Pakistan and later, President of Pakistan.

During the tenure of General Musharraf, a turning point of the history was the event of 9/11. After this event, Pakistan had to bring a huge change in its foreign policy. Parvez Musharraf opted the slogan of Pakistan first and changed policies accordingly.
General Parvez Musharraf (2001 - 2008)

Pakistan became the frontline player in the war against terrorism for which Pakistan also had to pay huge cost in the shape of loss of innocent lives, property and overall economy of the country. In 2002, Parvez Musharraf held referendum and became President of Pakistan. Later, general elections were held and Pakistan Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam) made the government.
General Parvez Musharraf (2001 - 2008)

Mir Zafarullah Khan Jamali became the first Prime Minister from Balochistan. Later, Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain and then Shoukat Aziz became Prime Ministers of Pakistan under Musharraf regime. In 2008, Pakistan People's Party formed government and Musharraf had to resign.

After the murder of Benazir Bhutto, Pakistan People's Party (PPP) won the elections and got back into power.
